Document ID: SRS-SA-005 | Version 1.0 | July 6, 2026

Cross-Cutting Concerns

Inventory Management System

Document Information

Attribute Detail
Document ID SRS-SA-006
Document Title Cross-Cutting Concerns — Inventory Management System
Version 1.0
Status Draft
Document Owner Solution Architect
Prepared For Development squads, security, DevOps, and QA leads
Date July 6, 2026
Classification Internal — Architecture Confidential
Scope Placement and responsibility of cross-cutting concerns across layers — no framework or library selection

Related Documents

Document ID Relationship
Layered Architecture Design SRS-SA-004 Four-layer model and dependency rule
System Modules Design SRS-SA-003 Identity & Access module (M-12)
Integration Architecture Design SRS-SA-005 Security zones and correlation IDs
Security Requirements NFR-SEC Authentication and authorization NFRs
Logging Requirements NFR-LOG Operational and audit logging NFRs
Compliance Requirements NFR-COM Audit trail and retention NFRs

Document Purpose

Cross-cutting concerns affect every module and layer of the Inventory Management System. This document identifies where each concern belongs in the Clean Architecture stack, what it must not do, and how concerns interact — so that security, auditability, and operational quality are implemented consistently without polluting domain logic.

1. Cross-Cutting Concerns Overview

1.1 Layer Placement Summary

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PRESENTATION     Auth middleware │ Input validators │ Exception filters    │
│                   Locale/format   │ Correlation ID attach                     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  APPLICATION      Authorization   │ Command/query  │ Transaction (UoW)     │
│                   behaviors       │ validation     │ Saga boundaries       │
│                   Exception map   │ Audit context  │ Cache policy (use)    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DOMAIN           Business        │ Domain         │ Domain exceptions     │
│                   invariants      │ validation     │ (rule violations)     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  INFRASTRUCTURE   Auth adapter    │ Logger         │ Cache implementation  │
│                   (IdP/SSO)      │ Audit writer   │ Config provider       │
│                   AuthZ adapter  │ Exception log  │ Localization resources│
│                   (M-12 port)    │ UoW impl       │ Transaction manager   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1.2 Concern Placement Matrix

Concern Primary Layer Supporting Layers Owning Module
Authentication Infrastructure Presentation, Application M-12 Identity & Access
Authorization Application Infrastructure (adapter), Domain (SoD rules) M-12 + M-03 Governance
Logging Infrastructure Presentation (correlation), Application (context) Platform (all modules)
Exception handling Presentation + Application Domain (throw), Infrastructure (log) Per module
Validation Domain + Presentation Application (orchestration) Per module
Auditing Infrastructure + Application Domain (events), Intelligence (projection) M-13 Intelligence
Caching Infrastructure Application (policy) M-04 Balance (ATP), M-13 Intelligence
Transactions Application Infrastructure (implementation) Per module
Configuration Infrastructure Application (inject) Platform
Localization Presentation + Infrastructure Application (formatting ports) Platform

2. Authentication

2.1 Definition in IMS

Authentication establishes who is performing an action — verifying that a user identity is genuine before any inventory command, query, or configuration change is accepted. Every transaction must be attributable to an individually authenticated user (NFR-SEC-001, NFR-SEC-002).

2.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation Extract credentials from incoming requests; attach authenticated principal to request context; reject unauthenticated requests before reaching handlers Auth middleware, session/token extractor, [Authorize] guards on controllers
Application Consume resolved UserId from context; never parse raw tokens; require identity for command attribution IUserContext port (read-only), command enrichment with UserId
Domain Accept UserId / UserActionAttribution as value objects on mutations; no authentication logic UserActionAttribution value object on aggregates
Infrastructure Integrate enterprise IdP (SSO); validate JWT/session; map claims to UserId; session store if required IdentityProviderAdapter, JwtTokenValidator, SessionStore

2.3 Module Ownership

Module Role
M-12 Identity & Access Owns user account lifecycle; defines authentication contract
All other modules Consume IUserContext / IIdentityService port — never implement auth

2.4 Key Rules

Rule Detail
AUTH-01 Zero shared accounts in production (NFR-SEC-001)
AUTH-02 Authentication occurs before any handler or controller business logic
AUTH-03 Re-authentication required for high-risk actions (NFR-SEC-004): bulk import, write-offs, role changes
AUTH-04 Failed login handling: lockout after 5 attempts / 15 minutes (NFR-SEC-003)
AUTH-05 Domain layer receives resolved identity only — never raw tokens or passwords

2.5 Does Not Belong In

  • Domain — authentication is an infrastructure concern; domain knows who acted, not how they proved identity
  • Other operational modules — no module except M-12 implements token validation

3. Authorization

3.1 Definition in IMS

Authorization determines what an authenticated user may do — role-based and location-scoped permissions across 100 system permissions and 19 business roles, plus segregation-of-duties enforcement (FR-084, FR-085, NFR-SEC-005 – NFR-SEC-009).

3.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation Optional coarse endpoint-level guards; delegate fine-grained checks to application layer Route-level role attributes (supplementary only)
Application Primary authorization gate — verify permission and location scope before every command handler; invoke SoD checks AuthorizationBehavior, RequirePermissionAttribute handler, LocationScopeBehavior
Domain Express SoD and eligibility as domain policies where business-meaningful; e.g., "counter cannot approve own count" SegregationOfDutiesPolicy, governance consultation
Infrastructure Implement IIdentityService / IAuthorizationService ports by delegating to M-12 Identity module adapter IdentityAuthorizationAdapter, permission cache (short TTL)

3.3 Policy Sources

Policy Type Defined In Enforced In
Role → permission matrix M-12 Identity Application layer AuthorizeAction
Location scope M-12 Identity + M-02 Network codes Application layer before location-scoped commands
Segregation of duties M-03 Governance + M-12 Identity Application layer at command; M-12 at role assignment
Business eligibility (e.g., discontinued SKU) Domain of owning module Domain layer invariants

3.4 Key Rules

Rule Detail
AUTHZ-01 Fail closed — if authorization cannot be determined, reject the command
AUTHZ-02 Authorization is checked in application layer, not in controllers alone
AUTHZ-03 Location-scoped roles validated against LocationCode on every warehouse command
AUTHZ-04 SoD violations blocked at role assignment (M-12) and at command execution (application)
AUTHZ-05 Read queries scoped to user's authorized locations and permissions

3.5 Does Not Belong In

  • Infrastructure (business rules) — permission matrix is not hard-coded in adapters
  • Domain (role checks) — domain enforces business SoD invariants, not RBAC matrix lookups

4. Logging

4.1 Definition in IMS

Logging captures operational diagnostic and security information — request traces, errors, performance markers, and security events — to support troubleshooting, monitoring (NFR-MON), and security investigation (NFR-LOG, NFR-SEC-025 – NFR-SEC-028).

Logging is distinct from auditing (Section 6) — logs are for operators; audit records are for compliance and governance.

4.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation Attach CorrelationId, RequestId, HTTP metadata to logging scope; log request start/end at info level Request logging middleware, correlation ID middleware
Application Enrich log scope with command name, aggregate ID, UserId; log handler entry/exit and saga steps Structured log context in behaviors, saga step logging
Domain No logging — domain remains pure; exceptions carry message codes only —
Infrastructure Logger implementation, log sinks, log format standard, retention, immutability for security logs StructuredLogger, log appenders, NFR-LOG-001 standard fields

4.3 Standard Log Attributes (NFR-LOG-001)

Every log entry includes: timestamp (UTC), severity, CorrelationId, UserId, module name, operation name, outcome, and duration where applicable.

Log Category Examples Retention
Operational Handler execution, query performance, cache hit/miss Per NFR-LOG retention schedule
Security Login success/failure, permission denied, SoD violation ≥ 7 years (NFR-COM-020)
Error Unhandled exceptions, saga compensation, integration failure Per operational schedule
Integration Cross-module port calls, ACL adapter requests, event publish Correlation-linked

4.4 Key Rules

Rule Detail
LOG-01 Domain layer does not write logs — keeps business logic testable and pure
LOG-02 Never log passwords, tokens, or full PII — mask sensitive fields (NFR-SEC-017)
LOG-03 Correlation ID propagates from presentation through application to infrastructure and cross-module calls
LOG-04 Security events logged at warn or higher; never suppressed
LOG-05 Log structure is consistent across all 13 modules

4.5 Does Not Belong In

  • Domain — no ILogger in aggregates
  • Audit trail — operational logs are not the compliance audit record (see Auditing)

5. Exception Handling

5.1 Definition in IMS

Exception handling manages the translation of failures — business rule violations, validation errors, authorization denials, and infrastructure faults — into controlled responses without exposing internal state or corrupting inventory data.

5.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation Catch application/domain exceptions; map to HTTP status and user-safe response DTOs; never expose stack traces to clients ExceptionFilter, ProblemDetails mapper, global exception handler
Application Catch infrastructure exceptions; wrap in application exceptions; trigger saga compensation; decide retry vs. fail Saga compensation handlers, CommandExceptionBehavior
Domain Throw domain exceptions for business rule violations — typed, meaningful, no HTTP concepts InsufficientAtpException, LocationFrozenException, SegregationOfDutiesViolationException
Infrastructure Log unhandled technical exceptions; translate persistence/network errors to infrastructure exceptions ORM exception wrapper, retry policies for transient DB errors

5.3 Exception Taxonomy

Exception Type Origin Layer HTTP Mapping (Presentation) User Message
ValidationException Presentation / Application 400 Bad Request Field-level errors
UnauthorizedException Application 401 Unauthorized Generic auth failure
ForbiddenException Application 403 Forbidden Insufficient permission
NotFoundException Application 404 Not Found Resource not found
BusinessRuleViolationException Domain 422 Unprocessable Entity Business-safe rule message
ConflictException Application / Domain 409 Conflict Concurrent modification, duplicate
InfrastructureException Infrastructure 503 Service Unavailable Generic system error

5.4 Saga and Exception Interaction

Scenario Handling
Reservation fails after order confirmed Saga compensates — CompensateOrderConfirmation
Put-away fails after receipt verified Receipt remains verified; put-away retried; no stock increase
Authorization denied mid-saga Saga aborts; no partial commits
Transient DB error Infrastructure retry; application remains unaware of retry count

5.5 Key Rules

Rule Detail
EXC-01 Domain throws domain exceptions — never returns error codes as return values
EXC-02 Presentation is the only layer that maps exceptions to HTTP
EXC-03 Business rule messages use ubiquitous language terms — not technical codes in user text
EXC-04 Unhandled exceptions logged at error with full correlation context
EXC-05 Exception handling never swallows stock mutation failures silently

5.6 Does Not Belong In

  • Domain — no HTTP status codes, no logging in catch blocks
  • Infrastructure — no business rule interpretation; wrap and rethrow

6. Validation

6.1 Definition in IMS

Validation ensures inputs and state transitions are well-formed and business-legal before execution. IMS distinguishes three validation levels — each belongs in a different layer.

6.2 Three Levels of Validation

Level Layer Scope Examples
Syntactic Presentation Request shape, types, required fields, format SKU not empty, quantity is positive integer, date parseable
Application Application Command preconditions, cross-field rules, saga guards "Approve adjustment" requires pending case ID; import batch size limit
Domain / Business Domain Invariants, business rules (BR-001 – BR-032) ATP ≥ 0, cannot reserve on frozen location, BR-019 SoD

6.3 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation Syntactic validation on request DTOs; return 400 before dispatching command Fluent validators, data annotations, request DTO rules
Application Application-level validation behaviors in command pipeline; consult governance/catalog/network ports for preconditions ValidationBehavior, command validators
Domain Authoritative business validation — invariants enforced in aggregate methods; cannot be bypassed Aggregate root methods, domain policies, specifications
Infrastructure Database constraints as last-resort safety net only — not primary validation Unique indexes, FK constraints, check constraints

6.4 Validation Pipeline (Command Path)

Request DTO
    │
    ▼
[Presentation]  Syntactic validation ──fail──► 400 Bad Request
    │
    ▼
[Application]     Authorization check
    │
    ▼
[Application]     Application precondition validation ──fail──► ValidationException
    │
    ▼
[Domain]          Aggregate method enforces invariants ──fail──► BusinessRuleViolationException
    │
    ▼
[Infrastructure]  Persist (DB constraints as safety net)

6.5 Key Rules

Rule Detail
VAL-01 Business rules live in domain — never only in UI or API validators
VAL-02 Presentation validation is for user experience — domain validation is for correctness
VAL-03 Validation rules from SRS-BR-001 and VR-xxx trace to domain invariants or application preconditions
VAL-04 Blind cycle count: application must not pass system quantity to presentation for counter view (BR-018)
VAL-05 Duplicate syntactic validation in domain is acceptable for defense in depth on critical invariants

6.6 Does Not Belong In

  • Infrastructure as primary validator — DB constraints supplement, not replace, domain rules
  • Presentation for business rules — UI cannot be the only enforcement of BR-001 (ATP)

7. Auditing

7.1 Definition in IMS

Auditing produces an immutable, governance-grade record of material inventory actions — who did what, when, where, why, and what changed — supporting BO-19 (100% audit trail), internal control (COSO), and external audit (NFR-COM-010, NFR-REL-009).

Auditing is not the same as operational logging. Audit records are structured business evidence; logs are diagnostic.

7.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation No audit logic — passes through authenticated context —
Application Enrich commands with audit context (UserId, reason code, correlation ID); collect domain events after successful commit AuditContextEnricher, post-handler event collection
Domain Raise domain events that constitute auditable business facts; embed UserActionAttribution on mutations StockReserved, AdjustmentApproved, attribution value objects
Infrastructure Persist audit records; implement append-only audit store; export evidence packages AuditTrailWriter, immutable log store
M-13 Intelligence Audit trail read projection — query, search, export for auditors (NFR-COM-012, NFR-PERF-026) AuditTrailProjection, ExportAuditEvidenceQueryHandler

7.3 Audit Record Sources

Source Mechanism Content
Domain events Event → Intelligence projection Business fact, before/after quantities, reason code
Command metadata Application layer audit context Initiator, approver, timestamp, location scope
Security events Infrastructure security log → audit projection Login, permission denied, role change
Governance decisions M-03 events Policy change, threshold amendment

7.4 Material Actions Requiring Audit (Non-Exhaustive)

Category Actions
Stock mutations Receipt, reservation, shipment, transfer, adjustment, write-off, quarantine
Governance Adjustment approval, write-off approval, policy change, reason code change
Master data Product lifecycle change, location activation/closure, supplier deactivation
Access Role assignment, SoD violation attempt, account deactivation
Count Cycle count result, physical count certification, variance approval
Financial Three-way match outcome, invoice authorization

7.5 Key Rules

Rule Detail
AUD-01 Audit records are append-only — no update or delete (NFR-LOG-026, NFR-COM-010)
AUD-02 Retained ≥ 7 years aligned with financial records (NFR-COM-019, NFR-COM-020)
AUD-03 Single authoritative audit projection in M-13 Intelligence — not duplicated per module
AUD-04 Domain events are the primary audit source — audit is a consequence of correct domain design
AUD-05 Auditor export within 15 minutes (NFR-PERF-026, NFR-COM-012)

7.6 Does Not Belong In

  • Presentation — no audit persistence in controllers
  • Operational logs as audit substitute — logs lack business structure and immutability guarantees
  • Per-module audit tables — centralized projection in Intelligence

8. Caching

8.1 Definition in IMS

Caching stores frequently accessed read data to meet performance NFRs — especially ATP lookup (NFR-PERF-002, 2 seconds) and dashboard load (NFR-PERF-004) — without serving stale data that could cause overselling.

8.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation HTTP cache headers for safe static resources only — not for ATP or stock data Static asset cache headers
Application Define cache use policy — when to read from cache vs. authoritative source; never cache write paths ICachePolicy consultation in query handlers
Domain No caching — domain always works with authoritative state —
Infrastructure Cache implementation, storage, TTL, invalidation on domain events AtpCacheService, DashboardCacheService, event-driven invalidation handlers

8.3 Cache Domains

Cache Target Owner Invalidation Trigger Staleness Tolerance
ATP by SKU/location M-04 Balance infrastructure StockReserved, StockReceived, StockShipped, StockAdjusted, quarantine events Near-zero — invalidate immediately on balance event
Product master M-01 Catalog infrastructure ProductUpdated, ProductLifecycleStatusChanged Minutes — catalog changes infrequently
Location status / freeze M-02 Network infrastructure LocationFreezeApplied, LocationFreezeReleased, activation events Near-zero for freeze; minutes for status
Dashboard KPIs M-13 Intelligence infrastructure Scheduled refresh + event-triggered for critical alerts Minutes (NFR-PERF-004)
Permission lookup M-12 Identity infrastructure RoleAssigned, RoleRevoked Short TTL (seconds) as safety net

8.4 Key Rules

Rule Detail
CACHE-01 Never cache write command paths — cache is read-only optimization
CACHE-02 ATP cache must invalidate on any balance change event — oversell risk
CACHE-03 Cache miss falls through to authoritative read repository — no fail-to-zero ATP
CACHE-04 Cached responses include asOf timestamp for channel feeds (EXT-03)
CACHE-05 Domain layer is cache-unaware — testability and correctness

8.5 Does Not Belong In

  • Domain — aggregates never read from cache
  • Application (implementation) — application defines policy; infrastructure implements store
  • Presentation — no in-memory ATP caching in controllers

9. Transactions

9.1 Definition in IMS

Transactions define atomicity boundaries — ensuring that one aggregate mutation completes fully or not at all, and that domain events are reliably published with the commit (outbox pattern).

9.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation No transaction management —
Application Own transaction boundaries — IUnitOfWork per command handler; one aggregate per transaction; saga spans multiple transactions IUnitOfWork, command handlers, saga orchestrators
Domain Define consistency within aggregate; no transaction awareness Aggregate atomic mutations
Infrastructure Implement IUnitOfWork, database connection, transaction manager, transactional outbox DbUnitOfWork, OutboxMessage persistence

9.3 Transaction Rules (DDD)

Rule Scope Detail
TX-01 Single command handler One UnitOfWork.Commit() per command — one aggregate mutation
TX-02 Cross-aggregate workflow Saga — each step is its own transaction; eventual consistency between steps
TX-03 Cross-module workflow Same as saga — no distributed transaction across modules
TX-04 Event publish Domain events written to outbox in same DB transaction as aggregate save
TX-05 Read queries No transaction required for CQRS read path; read-uncommitted not used for ATP
TX-06 Intelligence projections Separate transaction per projection handler — idempotent upsert

9.4 Transaction Flow

CommandHandler:
    UnitOfWork.Begin()
        aggregate = Repository.Get()
        aggregate.ExecuteCommand()     // domain invariants
        Repository.Save(aggregate)
        Outbox.Add(domainEvents)
    UnitOfWork.Commit()                // atomic: aggregate + outbox
    EventBus.Dispatch(outboxEvents)    // after commit

9.5 Key Rules

Rule Detail
TX-07 Application layer opens and commits transactions — not controllers, not domain
TX-08 Stock Position reservation and order confirmation are separate transactions linked by saga
TX-09 Retry of transient failures at infrastructure layer must not double-apply — idempotent handlers
TX-10 Long-running transactions prohibited — no transaction spans user think time or external API wait

9.6 Does Not Belong In

  • Domain — no BeginTransaction() in aggregates
  • Presentation — no request-scoped transactions across multiple commands
  • Distributed two-phase commit — prohibited across modules

10. Configuration

10.1 Definition in IMS

Configuration supplies environment-specific and tunable parameters — connection strings, feature flags, integration endpoints, threshold defaults, retention periods — without hard-coding them in domain or application logic.

10.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation UI display configuration only (e.g., page size defaults) — not system config View settings
Application Consume configuration via injected options interfaces — no direct file/env access IOptions<InventorySettings>, IFeatureManager
Domain No configuration — business thresholds that are governance policy live in M-03 Governance aggregate, not config files —
Infrastructure Load configuration from environment, secrets manager, config files; bind to options classes ConfigurationProvider, secrets adapter (SVC-07)

10.3 Configuration Categories

Category Examples Layer Mutable At Runtime
Infrastructure DB connection, IdP endpoint, email gateway Infrastructure Deploy time
Secrets API keys, certificates Infrastructure (secrets manager) Rotation via SVC-07
Feature flags Enable campaign module, bonded inventory Application (via infra provider) Yes — phased rollout
Operational tuning Cache TTL, saga timeout, retry count Application options Yes — ops tuning
Business policy Approval thresholds, reason codes M-03 Governance aggregate Via governance commands — not config file
Location-specific Business hours per location (NFR-AVL-005) M-02 Network master data Via location commands

10.4 Key Rules

Rule Detail
CFG-01 Business rules (BR-xxx) are domain/governance — not appsettings.json
CFG-02 Secrets never in source control or domain layer
CFG-03 Configuration injected via interfaces — application depends on IOptions<T>, not raw config
CFG-04 Feature flags control module activation per phased delivery — not compile-time branching
CFG-05 Location business hours are master data (M-02), not environment config

10.5 Does Not Belong In

  • Domain — no IConfiguration in aggregates
  • Governance thresholds in config files — use M-03 Governance Policy aggregate for auditability

11. Localization

11.1 Definition in IMS

Localization adapts user-facing text, number/date formats, and currency display for multi-region operations — without altering domain logic, business rules, or stored data formats.

11.2 Architectural Placement

Layer Responsibility Components
Presentation Primary localization — UI labels, messages, error text, report headers; culture selection from user preference or browser Resource files (.resx / i18n bundles), IStringLocalizer, culture middleware
Application Format dates and currency for query responses via abstraction — stored values remain UTC and canonical ILocalizationService, IDateTimeFormatter ports
Domain Culture-neutral — quantities, dates stored in canonical form (UTC, invariant decimal); reason codes stored as codes with localized display in presentation Canonical value objects only
Infrastructure Load resource bundles; provide localization service implementation LocalizationService, resource providers

11.3 Localization Scope

Localizable Not Localizable
UI labels and menus ProductSku, LocationCode identifiers
Validation error messages (presentation/application) Domain event names
Report column headers Audit trail stored values
User notification email templates Database-stored reason code keys (display localized separately)
Currency display format Monetary amounts stored in canonical decimal
Date display in user's timezone Timestamps stored UTC (NFR-LOG-001)

11.4 Key Rules

Rule Detail
L10N-01 Domain and persistence use invariant culture for all stored values
L10N-02 Business rule exception messages may carry message keys — presentation localizes for user display
L10N-03 Ubiquitous language terms (SRS-DM-008) are the source for translation keys — ATP, not "available stock" inconsistently
L10N-04 Audit and finance exports use locale-neutral formats for machine consumption; human reports may be localized
L10N-05 MVP may ship with single locale (English); architecture supports multi-locale without domain changes

11.5 Does Not Belong In

  • Domain — no culture-specific logic or translated strings in aggregates
  • Database — no per-locale duplicate master data rows for products

12. Cross-Cutting Pipeline (Command Request)

The following shows how all concerns interact on a single write request:

HTTP Request
    │
    ├─ [Presentation]  Correlation ID middleware
    ├─ [Presentation]  Authentication middleware ──────────► Infrastructure (IdP)
    ├─ [Presentation]  Localization (culture)
    ├─ [Presentation]  Syntactic validation
    │
    ▼
Command Bus
    │
    ├─ [Application]  Authorization behavior ───────────────► Infrastructure (M-12 port)
    ├─ [Application]  Application validation behavior
    ├─ [Application]  Audit context enrichment
    ├─ [Application]  Logging scope (command name, user)
    │
    ▼
Command Handler
    │
    ├─ [Application]  UnitOfWork.Begin()
    ├─ [Domain]       Aggregate enforces invariants
    ├─ [Infrastructure] Repository.Save + Outbox
    ├─ [Application]  UnitOfWork.Commit()
    ├─ [Infrastructure] Event bus dispatch
    ├─ [Infrastructure] Cache invalidation (if balance change)
    ├─ [Infrastructure] Audit projection update (M-13 handler)
    ├─ [Application]  Logging (success)
    │
    ▼
[Presentation]  Map result / Map exception ─────────────────► Client response

Concern Depends On Feeds Into

Authorization Authentication, M-12, M-03 Command execution gate
Validation — Domain execution or early rejection
Transactions — Event publish, Audit record
Auditing Authentication, Domain events Intelligence projection, Finance export
Logging Correlation ID Monitoring (NFR-MON)

14. Implementation Standards

ID Standard
CC-01 Cross-cutting behaviors implemented as ordered pipeline behaviors in application layer — not copy-pasted per handler
CC-02 All modules use shared cross-cutting libraries for logging format, exception types, correlation, and auth ports
CC-03 Domain layer projects have zero package references to logging, config, cache, or auth libraries
CC-04 Cross-cutting concerns tested independently — auth denial, validation failure, audit record creation
CC-05 NFR traceability maintained — each concern maps to specific NFR-SEC, NFR-LOG, NFR-COM requirements

Document Purpose

This document recommends a complete technology stack for the Inventory Management System. For each technology it provides purpose, selection rationale, alternatives considered, and trade-offs — enabling informed approval before project bootstrap.

2. Backend

2.1 Java 21 (LTS)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Primary programming language for all server-side domain, application, and infrastructure code
Why selected Mandated Java ecosystem; Java 21 is the current long-term support release with virtual threads (Project Loom) beneficial for I/O-bound warehouse API workloads; mature tooling and hiring pool for enterprise distribution/retail sector
Alternatives considered Java 17 LTS (still supported but misses virtual threads maturity); Kotlin on JVM (concise but splits team skill set)
Trade-offs (+) LTS stability, records/pattern matching, virtual threads for concurrency; (−) Slightly newer runtime than Java 17 — verify corporate JDK approval

2.2 Spring Boot 3.x

Aspect Detail
Purpose Application framework — dependency injection, auto-configuration, REST API, transaction management, actuator health endpoints, integration with entire Spring ecosystem
Why selected Mandated Spring stack; de facto enterprise standard; native support for security, data access, events, and testing; aligns with Clean Architecture via clear bean wiring of ports and adapters
Alternatives considered Quarkus (faster startup, smaller footprint — less mature Modulith support); Micronaut (compile-time DI — smaller community for DDD patterns); Plain Spring Framework without Boot (more boilerplate, slower bootstrap)
Trade-offs (+) Rapid development, extensive documentation, team familiarity; (−) Heavier runtime than Quarkus; requires discipline to avoid anemic Spring MVC + JPA anti-pattern — mitigated by Modulith and layered architecture

2.3 Spring Modulith

Aspect Detail
Purpose Enforces modular monolith boundaries — 13 bounded-context modules as separate Maven modules with compile-time dependency verification and module-scoped application events
Why selected Directly implements SRS-SA-002 (modular monolith) and SRS-SA-003 (13 modules); provides ApplicationModuleTest to verify acyclic module dependencies; supports event publication APIs and JDBC event registry for outbox; avoids premature microservices while preserving decomposition path
Alternatives considered Manual package-by-feature with ArchUnit only (works but no first-class event/outbox support); Microservices with Spring Cloud (rejected — ORC-04, BC-01); OSGi (obsolete complexity)
Trade-offs (+) Architecture-as-code module boundaries; event infrastructure built-in; (−) Relatively newer Spring project — smaller reference base than core Spring Boot; team training required

2.4 Spring Web (Spring MVC) + REST

Aspect Detail
Purpose Presentation layer — expose REST JSON APIs for Angular SPA, mobile warehouse clients, and Phase 2 external integrations
Why selected Standard Spring Boot stack; synchronous request-reply for ATP lookup (NFR-PERF-002, 2s target); well-understood by enterprise teams; integrates with Spring Security filter chain
Alternatives considered Spring WebFlux (reactive — adds complexity without clear benefit for CRUD + domain-heavy workloads); gRPC (efficient but poor browser compatibility for Angular); GraphQL (flexible queries but overkill for defined use cases)
Trade-offs (+) Simple mental model, excellent tooling, OpenAPI integration; (−) Thread-per-request model — mitigated by Java 21 virtual threads and connection pool tuning

2.5 MapStruct

Aspect Detail
Purpose Compile-time mapping between presentation DTOs, application commands/queries, and domain objects — keeps mapping out of controllers and handlers
Why selected Type-safe, zero-reflection overhead; aligns with Clean Architecture boundary mapping (SRS-SA-004); reduces boilerplate across 48 use cases
Alternatives considered ModelMapper (runtime reflection — harder to debug); Manual mapping (verbose, error-prone at scale); Dozer (legacy, maintenance declining)
Trade-offs (+) Fast, compile-time errors, readable generated code; (−) Annotation processor setup; learning curve for complex mappings

2.6 Springdoc OpenAPI

Aspect Detail
Purpose Auto-generate OpenAPI 3 specification from Spring MVC controllers — API contract documentation and Angular client generation
Why selected Standard for Spring Boot 3; supports contract-first collaboration between frontend and backend squads; enables Phase 2 CRM integration specification
Alternatives considered Springfox (unmaintained, incompatible with Spring Boot 3); Manual OpenAPI YAML (high maintenance)
Trade-offs (+) Always in sync with code; Swagger UI for QA; (−) Generated spec may need annotation tuning for clean contracts

3. Frontend

3.1 Angular 19

Aspect Detail
Purpose Single-page application framework for office users (purchasing, CS, management), warehouse web views, and system administration — all role-based IMS screens
Why selected Mandated frontend framework; enterprise-grade structure (modules, dependency injection, routing); strong TypeScript integration; long-term Google backing; suits large multi-team IMS with 90 functional requirements and role-based UI
Alternatives considered React (larger ecosystem but not mandated); Vue (lighter but less enterprise governance tooling); Blazor (requires .NET stack divergence)
Trade-offs (+) Opinionated structure aids consistency across squads; built-in routing, forms, HTTP; (−) Steeper learning curve than React; larger bundle — mitigated by lazy-loaded feature modules per bounded context

3.2 TypeScript 5.x

Aspect Detail
Purpose Typed language for Angular — compile-time safety for API contracts, form models, and state
Why selected Default and recommended language for Angular; reduces runtime errors in complex inventory forms (receipt lines, count entries, order lines)
Alternatives considered JavaScript (no type safety — unacceptable for 90 FRs scale)
Trade-offs (+) IDE support, refactoring safety; (−) Compilation step, type maintenance

3.3 Angular Material

Aspect Detail
Purpose UI component library — tables, forms, dialogs, navigation, data grids for inventory screens, dashboards, and approval workflows
Why selected Official Angular component library; accessible (WCAG); consistent enterprise look; data table and paginator suit stock inquiry and movement history screens
Alternatives considered PrimeNG (richer data components but third-party); NG-ZORRO (Ant Design — less common in Western enterprise); Custom CSS (slow, inconsistent)
Trade-offs (+) Maintained by Angular team, theming support; (−) Material Design aesthetic may need customization for corporate branding

3.4 RxJS + Angular Signals (Hybrid)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Reactive state and async data flow — HTTP API calls, real-time dashboard refresh, form debounce on SKU search (NFR-PERF-002)
Why selected RxJS is Angular's native async model; Angular 19 signals for local component state reduce boilerplate; hybrid approach suits ATP lookup streams and alert subscriptions
Alternatives considered NgRx (full Redux — overkill for MVP, adds ceremony); Plain promises (poor composition for complex UI flows)
Trade-offs (+) Powerful composition for search-as-you-type ATP; (−) RxJS learning curve — mitigate with shared service patterns and limited operator set

3.5 Angular PWA (Progressive Web App) — Warehouse Mobile

Aspect Detail
Purpose Installable web app for warehouse scanners and mobile devices — put-away, pick, cycle count without native app store deployment
Why selected BRD constraint TEC-03 (online MVP, no offline); PWA provides home-screen install, responsive layout, and camera/barcode API access on modern devices; single Angular codebase serves office and warehouse
Alternatives considered Native Android/iOS (higher cost, two codebases — BC-01); Ionic/Capacitor (adds layer — consider Phase 2 if scanner hardware integration deepens)
Trade-offs (+) One codebase, faster MVP, no app store; (−) Limited offline (acceptable per TEC-03); scanner hardware integration may need Capacitor plugin in Phase 2

4. Database

4.1 PostgreSQL 16

Aspect Detail
Purpose Primary relational database — transactional write store for all 13 modules, transactional outbox table, CQRS read projections, audit trail storage
Why selected Mandated database; ACID compliance critical for Stock Position invariants; excellent JSONB support for event payloads and flexible audit metadata; row-level locking for reservation contention; mature replication for read scaling; open source aligns with BC-01 fixed budget
Alternatives considered Microsoft SQL Server (licensing cost under BC-01); MySQL (weaker JSON and constraint tooling); Oracle (cost, overkill for mid-sized distribution); MongoDB (document model conflicts with aggregate transactional integrity)
Trade-offs (+) ACID, JSONB, partial indexes, logical replication, strong ecosystem; (−) Horizontal write scaling limited — acceptable for modular monolith MVP scale; team must manage vacuum/autovacuum tuning

4.2 Schema-per-Module (PostgreSQL Schemas)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Logical data isolation — each bounded-context module owns tables in a dedicated PostgreSQL schema (catalog, balance, fulfillment, etc.) enforcing SRS-SA-003 module boundary rule MB-07
Why selected Single PostgreSQL instance (operational simplicity ORC-04) with module ownership boundaries; prevents cross-module JOIN temptation; supports per-module Flyway migration scripts
Alternatives considered Single flat schema (no boundary enforcement); Database-per-module (microservices pattern — rejected); Separate databases per module (ops overhead)
Trade-offs (+) Module ownership clear, single backup target, ACID within instance; (−) Discipline required — no cross-schema FKs except shared kernel reference tables

4.3 Flyway

Aspect Detail
Purpose Version-controlled database migration — schema evolution per module, repeatable across environments and location rollouts
Why selected SQL-first migrations align with DBA review practices; Spring Boot native integration; per-module migration locations map to Spring Modulith structure
Alternatives considered Liquibase (XML/YAML abstraction — more flexible but heavier); Hibernate ddl-auto (prohibited for production — no governance)
Trade-offs (+) Simple, auditable SQL scripts, CI integration; (−) No automatic rollback — requires forward-fix migration discipline

4.4 Redis 7 (Supplementary Cache Store)

Aspect Detail
Purpose In-memory cache for ATP hot-path queries (NFR-PERF-002), optional session store, rate limiting counters — not system of record
Why selected Sub-millisecond read for high-frequency SKU availability lookups; event-driven invalidation from Balance module domain events (SRS-SA-006 caching rules); offloads PostgreSQL read pressure during peak season (NFR-AVL-003)
Alternatives considered Caffeine (in-process only — invalid in multi-instance deployment); PostgreSQL materialized views alone (insufficient for 2s SLA under concurrent load); Hazelcast (heavier operational footprint)
Trade-offs (+) Proven, fast, TTL and pub/sub for invalidation; (−) Additional infrastructure component; cache staleness risk — mitigated by event invalidation and asOf timestamp

5. ORM

5.1 Hibernate ORM 6 (via Spring Data JPA)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Object-relational mapping — persist and hydrate domain aggregates via repository implementations in infrastructure layer; not exposed to domain layer
Why selected Default JPA provider in Spring Boot 3; mature PostgreSQL dialect; supports optimistic locking (@Version) for Stock Position contention; Spring Data JPA reduces repository boilerplate; team familiarity in Java enterprise
Alternatives considered MyBatis (SQL-centric — more control but mapping drifts from domain model); jOOQ (excellent for complex queries and CQRS read side — consider supplement for Intelligence module); EclipseLink (less Spring community momentum); Raw JDBC (too low-level for 18 aggregates)
Trade-offs (+) Productivity, Spring integration, optimistic locking, auditing (@CreatedBy); (−) Risk of anemic domain model and lazy-loading leaks — mitigated by: aggregates mapped explicitly, repository interfaces in domain, no entity exposure past infrastructure, ArchUnit rules

5.2 Spring Data JPA (Repository Abstraction)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Implement IStockPositionRepository and other domain repository ports — query methods, custom @Query for complex reads, pagination for movement history
Why selected Standard Spring stack; reduces CRUD boilerplate for master data modules (Catalog, Network, Governance); integrates with @Transactional unit of work
Alternatives considered Plain Hibernate Session API (more verbose); Spring Data JDBC (no lazy loading — simpler but less aggregate mapping support)
Trade-offs (+) Convention over configuration; (−) Derived query methods can hide expensive queries — require query review and EXPLAIN analysis for ATP paths

5.3 jOOQ (Supplementary — Intelligence Read Side)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Type-safe SQL for CQRS read projections in M-13 Intelligence — complex KPI queries, audit trail search, dashboard aggregations without loading JPA entities
Why selected Reporting queries must not burden JPA entity model (AR-10); jOOQ generates type-safe SQL from PostgreSQL schema; complements JPA on write side
Alternatives considered Native SQL in @Query (untyped, error-prone); PostgreSQL views only (limited composability in application)
Trade-offs (+) Performance, type safety for read models; (−) Second data access pattern — limit to Intelligence module only

6. Security

6.1 Spring Security 6

Aspect Detail
Purpose Application security framework — authentication filter chain, authorization rules, CSRF protection, method-level security, session management
Why selected Industry standard for Spring Boot; implements SRS-SA-006 authentication and authorization placement; integrates with OAuth2/OIDC resource server; supports location-scoped permission expressions
Alternatives considered Apache Shiro (less Spring-native); Custom JWT filter (reinventing maintained library); Keycloak adapters deprecated in favor of OAuth2 resource server pattern
Trade-offs (+) Comprehensive, well-documented, NFR-SEC alignment; (−) Configuration complexity — mitigate with shared security module and tested config

6.2 OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect (OIDC)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Enterprise SSO integration with identity provider (SVC-01) — Entra ID, Okta, or LDAP-federated OIDC; JWT bearer tokens for Angular SPA and API
Why selected NFR-SEC-001 (unique user authentication); no shared accounts; standard protocol supported by all enterprise IdPs; Angular angular-oauth2-oidc library mature
Alternatives considered SAML 2.0 (legacy, XML-heavy — still supported but OIDC preferred for SPA); Session-only form login (no SSO, poor for enterprise); API keys (insufficient for user attribution)
Trade-offs (+) Enterprise SSO, token-based stateless API, refresh token flow; (−) Token management complexity in Angular; requires IdP provisioning process for 19 roles

6.3 JWT Resource Server

Aspect Detail
Purpose Validate JWT access tokens on every API request; extract claims for UserId, roles, and location scope; stateless API authentication
Why selected Aligns with Angular SPA architecture; scales horizontally without server-side session affinity; supports NFR-SEC-021 session management policies
Alternatives considered Server-side sessions with Redis (stateful — works but adds session management overhead); Basic auth (prohibited — NFR-SEC-001)
Trade-offs (+) Stateless, cloud-friendly; (−) Token revocation requires short TTL + refresh or token blocklist for immediate deprovision

6.4 BCrypt / DelegatingPasswordEncoder

Aspect Detail
Purpose Password hashing for locally provisioned accounts (fallback when SSO unavailable) and service account secrets
Why selected Spring Security default; NFR-SEC-010 password policy compliance; adaptive cost factor
Alternatives considered Argon2 (stronger — supported via DelegatingPasswordEncoder if policy requires); Plain hash (prohibited)
Trade-offs (+) Built-in, proven; (−) BCrypt 72-byte limit — irrelevant for generated passwords

7. Messaging

7.1 Spring Application Events + Spring Modulith Event API (MVP)

Aspect Detail
Purpose In-process domain event bus for MVP — cross-module choreography within modular monolith (SRS-SA-005); PutAwayCompleted → Balance, all events → Intelligence
Why selected No external broker ops for MVP (ORC-04); Spring Modulith provides module-scoped event publication and subscription; transactional integrity with JDBC event registry; meets internal event latency < 5 seconds
Alternatives considered RabbitMQ/Kafka from day one (ops overhead, BC-01); Direct method calls (tight coupling — violates module boundaries); Database polling only (higher latency)
Trade-offs (+) Zero additional infrastructure, ACID with outbox, simple debugging; (−) Not suitable for external system integration — Phase 2 broker required for CRM webhooks and channel feeds

7.2 Transactional Outbox (PostgreSQL + Spring Modulith JDBC Registry)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Reliable domain event delivery — events written to outbox table in same transaction as aggregate save; async dispatcher publishes after commit (SRS-SA-005, NFR-REL-007)
Why selected Prevents lost events on crash between DB commit and publish; idempotent event handlers; supports at-least-once delivery with deduplication by EventId
Alternatives considered Dual-write (publish then save — inconsistent); XA two-phase commit (complex, performance penalty); Change Data Capture / Debezium (ops heavy for MVP)
Trade-offs (+) Proven pattern, uses existing Postgre PostgreSQL; (−) Outbox table growth — requires archival job; slight publish latency (acceptable)

7.3 RabbitMQ (Phase 2 — Recommended External Broker)

Aspect Detail
Purpose External async integration — CRM order webhooks, channel ATP feed, finance export triggers, notification dispatch; decouple IMS from external consumer pace
Why selected Mature, operable by limited IT team; sufficient throughput for IMS scale; Spring AMQP integration; easier ops than Kafka for mid-sized message volumes
Alternatives considered Apache Kafka (higher throughput, event replay — overkill for MVP scale, steeper ops ORC-04); AWS SQS (cloud lock-in); Redis Streams (less durable guarantee)
Trade-offs (+) Proven, Spring integration, manageable ops; (−) Not ideal for event sourcing replay at scale — acceptable as IMS uses PostgreSQL as source of truth, not broker log

Final broker selection deferred to Phase 2 integration workshop (HS-014, EXT-01).

8. Build Tools

8.1 Apache Maven (Multi-Module)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Build orchestration — multi-module project structure mapping to 13 bounded contexts + shared kernel + application shell; dependency management, packaging, CI integration
Why selected Enterprise standard for Java/Spring; explicit XML configuration aids governance review; Spring Modulith documentation uses Maven; predictable CI pipeline; wide IDE support
Alternatives considered Gradle (faster builds, Kotlin DSL — preferred by some teams but less universal in enterprise procurement environments); Bazel (overkill); Single-module build (no boundary enforcement)
Trade-offs (+) Universal, stable, audit-friendly pom.xml; (−) Slower than Gradle; verbose XML — mitigate with parent POM and BOM

8.2 Spring Boot Maven BOM

Aspect Detail
Purpose Centralized dependency version management — aligned Spring Boot, Spring Security, Hibernate, Jackson versions across all modules
Why selected Prevents version conflicts across 13 modules; Spring-tested compatibility matrix
Alternatives considered Manual version pinning per module (drift risk)
Trade-offs (+) Consistency, security patch alignment; (−) Tied to Spring Boot release cadence

8.3 GitHub Actions / Azure DevOps Pipelines (CI/CD)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Continuous integration — build, test, ArchUnit boundary checks, Flyway validation, Docker image publish on merge
Why selected Automated quality gate for 13-module codebase; supports parallel module test execution; organization likely has existing pipeline platform
Alternatives considered Jenkins (self-hosted ops overhead); GitLab CI (depends on repo hosting)
Trade-offs (+) Automated NFR regression via test suite; (−) Pipeline maintenance — shared templates reduce per-module duplication

9. Testing

9.1 JUnit 5

Aspect Detail
Purpose Unit and integration test framework — domain invariant tests, command handler tests, repository tests
Why selected Java standard; Spring Boot Test native support; parameterized tests for business rule matrices (BR-001 – BR-032)
Alternatives considered TestNG (less Spring ecosystem momentum); Spock/Groovy (different language)
Trade-offs (+) Universal, IDE support; (−) Verbose compared to Spock — acceptable

9.2 Mockito

Aspect Detail
Purpose Mock domain repository ports and cross-module query ports in application layer unit tests — isolate handlers from infrastructure
Why selected Standard Java mocking; aligns with Clean Architecture testing (SRS-SA-004 LS-10)
Alternatives considered WireMock (for HTTP — use for ACL adapter tests); Manual stubs (verbose)
Trade-offs (+) Fast unit tests; (−) Over-mocking risk — balance with integration tests

9.3 Spring Boot Test + Testcontainers

Aspect Detail
Purpose Integration tests with real PostgreSQL and Redis in Docker containers — verify repository mappings, Flyway migrations, saga flows, and outbox delivery
Why selected Eliminates H2/embedded DB divergence from PostgreSQL production behaviour; Testcontainers is industry standard for Spring integration tests
Alternatives considered H2 in-memory (PostgreSQL incompatibility — JSONB, locking); Dedicated test database (CI hygiene issues)
Trade-offs (+) Production-parity testing; (−) Slower CI — mitigate with test slicing and parallel execution

9.4 ArchUnit

Aspect Detail
Purpose Architecture fitness functions — enforce module boundary rules (SRS-SA-003 MB-01 – MB-08), layer dependency rule (SRS-SA-004), domain purity (no JPA in domain package)
Why selected Prevents modular monolith erosion; automated gate in CI; complements Spring Modulith module tests
Alternatives considered Manual code review only (insufficient at scale); jQAssistant (heavier graph analysis)
Trade-offs (+) Automated architecture governance; (−) Rules require maintenance as packages evolve

9.5 Cypress (E2E — Angular)

Aspect Detail
Purpose End-to-end browser tests for critical user journeys — ATP lookup, goods receipt, order reservation, cycle count blind entry
Why selected Strong Angular integration; readable tests for QA collaboration; supports warehouse responsive viewport testing
Alternatives considered Playwright (excellent, growing — either acceptable); Selenium (verbose, flaky); Protractor (deprecated)
Trade-offs (+) Developer-friendly, good debugging; (−) Slower than unit tests — limit to MVP critical path suite (~20 journeys)

9.6 k6 / Gatling (Performance — Phase 2)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Load testing for NFR-PERF validation — concurrent ATP lookups, reservation contention on Class A SKUs, peak season simulation
Why selected Validates NFR-PERF-001 – NFR-PERF-003 before go-live; k6 scriptable in CI
Alternatives considered JMeter (GUI-heavy, less CI-friendly)
Trade-offs (+) Evidence for capacity model; (−) Deferred to pre-go-live phase per NFR performance baseline program

10. Containerization

10.1 Docker

Aspect Detail
Purpose Package IMS application, Angular static assets (via nginx sidecar or embedded), and local development dependencies (PostgreSQL, Redis) as portable containers
Why selected Industry standard; consistent dev/prod parity; required for Testcontainers; supports ORC-04 limited ops via immutable deployments
Alternatives considered Bare JAR deployment (environment drift); VM images (heavier, slower iteration)
Trade-offs (+) Reproducible, portable, CI-friendly; (−) Team Docker literacy required; image security scanning needed

10.2 Docker Compose (Development & Integration Test)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Local developer environment — Spring Boot app + PostgreSQL + Redis + mail catcher (notifications) with single docker compose up
Why selected Fast onboarding for mixed-skill delivery team; mirrors integration test environment
Alternatives considered Local native PostgreSQL install (inconsistent versions); Devcontainers (optional supplement)
Trade-offs (+) One-command environment; (−) Not for production — production uses orchestrator

10.3 Kubernetes (Production — Phase 2+)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Production orchestration — horizontal pod autoscaling for API tier, rolling deployments for zero-downtime location rollouts (OC-01), health checks (NFR-AVL-001)
Why selected Cloud platform standard (SVC-04); supports 99.5% uptime with replica sets; secrets via SVC-07 integration
Alternatives considered Managed PaaS (Azure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk — simpler ops, recommended for MVP if ORC-04 is critical); Docker Swarm (declining adoption)
Trade-offs (+) Scalable, self-healing, industry standard; (−) Operational complexity — recommend managed Kubernetes (AKS/EKS) or PaaS for MVP, defer full K8s ops to Phase 2

10.4 Nginx (Static Asset Serving)

Aspect Detail
Purpose Serve Angular production build; reverse proxy to Spring Boot API; TLS termination at edge
Why selected Lightweight, proven; separates static frontend from API scaling
Alternatives considered Spring Boot serving static files (couples frontend deploy to backend); CDN only (premature for internal IMS)
Trade-offs (+) Clean separation, cache headers for static assets; (−) Additional container in deployment

11. Observability Stack (Supplementary)

Technology Purpose Why Selected
Micrometer Application metrics facade Spring Boot Actuator native; NFR-MON KPI metrics
Prometheus Metrics collection and storage Industry standard; scrape Spring Actuator /actuator/prometheus
Grafana Dashboards and alerting Ops visibility; NFR-MON-001 5-minute outage detection
Logback + JSON encoder Structured logging NFR-LOG-001 standard fields; ELK/Loki ingestion ready
OpenTelemetry Distributed tracing Correlation ID propagation across modules (SRS-SA-006)

ims-parent/                          (BOM, dependency management)
├── ims-shared-kernel/               (ProductSku, LocationCode, shared events envelope)
├── ims-catalog/                     (M-01)
│   ├── catalog-domain/
│   ├── catalog-application/
│   ├── catalog-infrastructure/
│   └── catalog-api/                 (REST controllers — presentation)
├── ims-balance/                     (M-04 — core domain)
