Inventory Management System Navigation Structure

Purpose

This document defines the application's navigation structure for the Inventory Management System. It is based on the approved BRD, use cases, API design, and the screen inventory. It describes how users move through the application but does not define visual layout or page wireframes.

Navigation Model

  • Primary navigation: Persistent top-level modules used to move across major business domains.
  • Secondary navigation: Section-level navigation within a selected module.
  • Breadcrumbs: Hierarchical path showing where the user is and enabling quick backtracking.
  • Contextual navigation: In-page task links, related records, status-driven actions, and work queues.
  • Role-specific menus: Navigation visibility and priority adapted to each user role.

Main Navigation

The main navigation should present the following top-level modules:

  1. Home
  2. Inventory
  3. Products
  4. Locations
  5. Procurement
  6. Inbound
  7. Fulfillment
  8. Transfers
  9. Returns
  10. Reports & Analytics
  11. Governance & Audit
  12. Administration

Supporting persistent utilities:

  • Notifications
  • Global Search
  • My Tasks / Approvals
  • User Menu / Session

Secondary Navigation

Secondary navigation should appear after a user enters a main module.

Home

  • Operational Dashboard
  • Executive KPI Dashboard
  • My Notifications
  • My Approvals

Inventory

  • Inventory Status Monitor
  • Availability Inquiry
  • Movement History
  • Cycle Counts
  • Physical Counts
  • Variance Approvals
  • Stock Adjustments
  • Write-Offs
  • Quarantine & Holds
  • Shrinkage & Obsolescence

Products

  • Product Catalog
  • Product Import
  • ABC Classification
  • Stock Policies

Locations

  • Location Directory
  • Location Hierarchy
  • Storage Positions
  • Location Activation / Closure

Procurement

  • Suppliers
  • Purchase Requisitions
  • Purchase Orders
  • Inbound Delivery Planning
  • Inbound Supply Tracking
  • Low-Stock Alerts
  • Replenishment Planning

Inbound

  • Goods Receipt Workbench
  • Receipt Discrepancies
  • Put-Away Workbench
  • Non-PO Receipt Intake

Fulfillment

  • Order Reservation
  • Pick / Pack / Ship
  • Partial Fulfillment & Backorders
  • Fulfillment Exceptions
  • Order Status
  • Multi-Location Fulfillment

Transfers

  • Transfer Requests
  • Transfer Approvals
  • Transfer Execution
  • In-Transit Tracking
  • Network Rebalancing

Returns

  • Return Authorizations
  • Return Inspection & Disposition

Reports & Analytics

  • Operational Reports
  • Inventory Dashboard
  • KPI Dashboard
  • Valuation Reconciliation
  • Promotional Readiness

Governance & Audit

  • Governance Policies
  • Reason Codes
  • Audit Workspace
  • Audit Trail Query
  • Approvals Inbox

Administration

  • User Accounts
  • Roles & Access Control

Breadcrumbs

Breadcrumbs should reflect the navigation hierarchy in the format:

Home > Module > Section > Record / Action

Examples:

  • Home > Inventory > Inventory Status Monitor
  • Home > Products > Product Catalog > SKU-100245
  • Home > Procurement > Purchase Orders > PO-2026-00418
  • Home > Inbound > Goods Receipt Workbench > GR-2026-00291
  • Home > Fulfillment > Order Status > SO-2026-01872
  • Home > Transfers > Transfer Requests > TR-2026-00088
  • Home > Returns > Return Authorizations > RA-2026-00116
  • Home > Governance & Audit > Audit Trail Query > Export Results
  • Home > Administration > User Accounts > User Profile > Edit Role Assignments

Breadcrumb behavior:

  • The first crumb should always return to Home.
  • Intermediate crumbs should return to the parent list or workspace.
  • The final crumb should represent the current screen, record, or action state.
  • Modal or side-panel actions should not replace the breadcrumb unless they open as full screens.

Contextual Navigation

Contextual navigation should be available within screens to help users complete related tasks without returning to module menus.

Inventory contexts

  • From Inventory Status Monitor:
    • View Product
    • View Location
    • Open Movement History
    • Create Adjustment
    • Request Transfer
    • Open Replenishment Planning

Product contexts

  • From Product Catalog or a product detail:
    • Edit Product
    • View Stock by Location
    • Open Stock Policy
    • Open ABC Classification
    • View Movement History
    • Import Related Data

Procurement contexts

  • From Low-Stock Alerts:
    • Acknowledge Alert
    • Review Network Availability
    • Create Requisition
    • Create Transfer Request
  • From Purchase Requisition:
    • Approve
    • Reject
    • Convert to PO

Inbound contexts

  • From Goods Receipt Workbench:
    • Verify Receipt
    • Log Discrepancy
    • Send to Put-Away
    • View PO

Fulfillment contexts

  • From Order Reservation:
    • Check Availability
    • Reserve Stock
    • Release Reservation
    • Open Split Fulfillment
  • From Pick / Pack / Ship:
    • Verify Pick
    • View Lot / Batch
    • Raise Exception
    • Confirm Shipment

Transfer contexts

  • From Transfer Request:
    • Approve / Reject
    • View Source Capacity
    • Dispatch Transfer
    • Receive Transfer

Returns contexts

  • From Return Authorization:
    • View Original Order
    • Receive Return
    • Inspect Return
    • Disposition Return

Audit and admin contexts

  • From Audit Trail Query:
    • Open Record
    • Export Evidence
  • From User Account Management:
    • Assign Role
    • Suspend User
    • Deactivate User
    • View Access Scope

Navigation Principles

  1. Home should act as the universal return point for all roles.
  2. Modules should reflect business domains, not technical services.
  3. Work-queue screens should be reachable from both module navigation and My Tasks / Approvals.
  4. High-frequency operational screens should be no more than two clicks from the main navigation.
  5. Role-based visibility should hide irrelevant modules rather than merely disabling them.
  6. Contextual links should connect adjacent workflows such as alert to requisition, receipt to discrepancy, and order to shipment.

Inventory Management System User Journeys

Purpose

This document defines user journeys for the major business processes in the Inventory Management System. Each journey is written from the user's perspective and focuses on the user's goal, decision points, friction, and successful outcome rather than internal system behavior.

Scope

The journeys below cover the major business processes defined in the approved BRD:

  1. Product master data management
  2. Location and warehouse setup
  3. Stock policy and threshold definition
  4. Goods receipt and verification
  5. Receipt discrepancy resolution
  6. Stock put-away
  7. Inventory status monitoring
  8. Inventory availability inquiry
  9. Cycle counting
  10. Full physical inventory count
  11. Variance investigation and approval
  12. Stock adjustment
  13. Inventory write-off
  14. Quarantine and hold management
  15. Order availability confirmation
  16. Inventory reservation
  17. Pick, pack, and ship
  18. Partial fulfillment and backorder handling
  19. Low-stock alert review
  20. Replenishment planning
  21. Inter-location transfer request
  22. Transfer approval
  23. Transfer execution
  24. Customer return authorization
  25. Return inspection and disposition
  26. Reporting and operational review
  27. Inventory valuation reconciliation
  28. Promotional stock readiness
  29. Audit and control review
  30. User account and access management

1. Product Master Data Management

  • User role: Inventory Controller
  • Goal: Create or maintain an accurate product record so every team works from one trusted SKU definition.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the product catalog.
    2. Search for the product to confirm it does not already exist.
    3. Create a new product or open an existing one for update.
    4. Enter or revise SKU, name, category, unit of measure, barcode, and status.
    5. Review the record for completeness.
    6. Save the product and confirm it is available for operations.
  • Decisions:
    • Is this a new product or an update to an existing one?
    • Is there a possible duplicate that should be resolved before saving?
    • Should the product be active, inactive, or discontinued?
  • Pain points:
    • Duplicate products create confusion and downstream errors.
    • Missing attributes can block receiving, reservation, or reporting later.
    • Product status decisions may affect purchasing and sales unexpectedly.
  • Success outcome: A complete, unique, and trusted product record is available for all inventory processes.

2. Location and Warehouse Setup

  • User role: Inventory Controller
  • Goal: Configure a location correctly so stock can be assigned, counted, received, moved, and reported there.
  • Steps:
    1. Open location management.
    2. Create a new location or update an existing one.
    3. Define the location type, hierarchy, and operational status.
    4. Configure storage positions if needed.
    5. Load or confirm opening balances for go-live.
    6. Activate the location for daily operations.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the location operationally ready for activation?
    • Does it belong under an existing parent location?
    • Are opening balances verified enough to trust the location at go-live?
  • Pain points:
    • Poor setup causes inventory to be tracked in the wrong place.
    • Unclear hierarchy can affect reporting and transfer flows.
    • Inaccurate opening balances create immediate mistrust in the system.
  • Success outcome: The location is correctly configured, active, and ready for controlled stock activity.

3. Stock Policy and Threshold Definition

  • User role: Inventory Controller
  • Goal: Set thresholds that help the business replenish on time without overstocking.
  • Steps:
    1. Open stock policy management.
    2. Find the product and relevant location.
    3. Review current stock levels, demand expectations, and service needs.
    4. Set reorder level, minimum threshold, and safety stock.
    5. Save the policy.
    6. Confirm the policy is active for monitoring and alerts.
  • Decisions:
    • Does this product need a location-specific policy?
    • Is current safety stock sufficient or too conservative?
    • Should thresholds change because demand or lead time changed?
  • Pain points:
    • Users may lack confidence in the data behind threshold decisions.
    • Overly low thresholds increase stockout risk.
    • Overly high thresholds tie up working capital.
  • Success outcome: The product is governed by clear thresholds that support proactive replenishment.

4. Goods Receipt and Verification

  • User role: Receiving Clerk
  • Goal: Receive incoming supplier goods accurately so only verified stock enters inventory.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the goods receipt workbench.
    2. Locate the expected purchase order or shipment.
    3. Scan or enter received items.
    4. Verify item identity, quantity, and visible condition.
    5. Capture lot, batch, or shelf-life details when required.
    6. Confirm the receipt and stage stock for put-away.
  • Decisions:
    • Does the shipment match the purchase order?
    • Is there damage, shortage, wrong product, or shelf-life issue?
    • Can the receipt be accepted as normal or does it require discrepancy handling?
  • Pain points:
    • Matching paperwork to physical goods can be slow.
    • Traceable products add extra data-entry pressure.
    • Receiving the wrong item creates immediate process interruption.
  • Success outcome: Verified goods are accurately received and ready for the next step without compromising stock accuracy.

5. Receipt Discrepancy Resolution

  • User role: Receiving Clerk
  • Goal: Record and resolve inbound differences without losing supplier accountability or inventory control.
  • Steps:
    1. Identify a mismatch during receiving.
    2. Open discrepancy logging for the affected receipt line.
    3. Record discrepancy type, quantity impact, and notes.
    4. Attach evidence if needed.
    5. Escalate for manager review or resolution.
    6. Complete the receipt with accepted quantities and documented variance.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the issue a shortage, overage, wrong item, damage, or tolerance breach?
    • Should the quantity be accepted, partially accepted, or held for review?
    • Does the discrepancy require manager approval or supplier follow-up?
  • Pain points:
    • Users can feel pressured to keep receiving moving quickly.
    • Incomplete evidence makes later disputes harder to resolve.
    • Rework increases when discrepancies are documented inconsistently.
  • Success outcome: The discrepancy is fully documented, the accepted stock is correct, and the issue can be followed through to closure.

6. Stock Put-Away

  • User role: Warehouse Staff
  • Goal: Move received goods into the correct storage location so they become available for fulfillment and tracking.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the put-away task queue.
    2. Select the next receipt awaiting storage.
    3. Move goods from receiving to the suggested storage position.
    4. Confirm product, quantity, and storage location.
    5. Complete put-away confirmation.
    6. Verify the task is cleared from the queue.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the suggested location appropriate and available?
    • Does product rotation require FIFO or FEFO handling?
    • Is there any mismatch between the staged quantity and the physical goods?
  • Pain points:
    • Storage congestion can force manual workaround decisions.
    • Incorrect placement causes future pick failures and count problems.
    • Staff may lose time if receiving and storage labeling are unclear.
  • Success outcome: Stock is in the right location, properly recorded, and available for downstream use.

7. Inventory Status Monitoring

  • User role: Inventory Controller
  • Goal: Understand overall stock health and identify issues before they disrupt operations.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the inventory status monitor.
    2. Filter by location, product type, or status.
    3. Review low-stock, out-of-stock, overstock, and quarantined items.
    4. Drill into a product or location when something looks wrong.
    5. Decide whether follow-up action is needed.
    6. Route the issue to replenishment, transfer, adjustment, or investigation.
  • Decisions:
    • Is this a temporary issue or something that requires immediate action?
    • Should the next action be replenishment, transfer, or investigation?
    • Is the problem local to one location or network-wide?
  • Pain points:
    • Users may see symptoms before they see the root cause.
    • Too many alerts can make prioritization difficult.
    • Network-level visibility can be overwhelming without filtering.
  • Success outcome: The user quickly identifies stock risks and knows what action to take next.

8. Inventory Availability Inquiry

  • User role: Sales Representative
  • Goal: Answer a customer stock question confidently without needing to call the warehouse.
  • Steps:
    1. Open availability inquiry.
    2. Search by SKU, product name, or barcode.
    3. Review on-hand, reserved, and ATP figures.
    4. Check relevant locations or network-wide availability.
    5. Confirm stock status and expected inbound if needed.
    6. Respond to the customer.
  • Decisions:
    • Is there enough ATP to support a commitment?
    • Should the answer be location-specific or network-wide?
    • Is expected inbound relevant to the customer conversation?
  • Pain points:
    • Users need fast answers during live customer conversations.
    • Confusion between on-hand and ATP can lead to bad promises.
    • If stock is fragmented across locations, the answer may be less straightforward.
  • Success outcome: The customer receives a fast, accurate, and credible availability answer.

9. Cycle Counting

  • User role: Warehouse Staff
  • Goal: Count assigned stock accurately without being biased by system quantities.
  • Steps:
    1. Open assigned cycle counts.
    2. Go to the specified product and storage location.
    3. Count the physical stock.
    4. Enter the counted quantity.
    5. Submit the result.
    6. Move to the next assignment.
  • Decisions:
    • Does the physical stock clearly match one count result, or should it be recounted?
    • Is the storage area clear enough to count confidently?
    • Should an unusual condition be noted for later investigation?
  • Pain points:
    • Cluttered or mixed storage slows counting.
    • Staff may worry about making mistakes that trigger investigations.
    • Repeated counting tasks can feel disruptive to warehouse throughput.
  • Success outcome: The physical count is submitted accurately and supports improved inventory confidence.

10. Full Physical Inventory Count

  • User role: Inventory Controller
  • Goal: Complete a controlled wall-to-wall count that establishes a trusted inventory baseline.
  • Steps:
    1. Start a physical inventory count session.
    2. Confirm the location is frozen for normal movement.
    3. Assign teams or zones for counting.
    4. Monitor progress as counts are entered.
    5. Identify any incomplete or questionable areas.
    6. Close and certify the count session.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the location ready to enter freeze mode?
    • Are all areas fully counted and verified?
    • Can the count be certified now or should unresolved issues be addressed first?
  • Pain points:
    • Full counts are operationally disruptive.
    • Users must coordinate many people under time pressure.
    • Incomplete counts reduce trust in the final result.
  • Success outcome: The location completes a reliable full count and generates a trustworthy variance baseline.

11. Variance Investigation and Approval

  • User role: Warehouse Manager
  • Goal: Understand why a count variance happened and approve only justified corrections.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the pending variance queue.
    2. Select a variance case.
    3. Review system quantity versus counted quantity.
    4. Investigate likely causes with notes and evidence.
    5. Decide whether to approve, escalate, or reject the proposed correction.
    6. Route the case to the proper next step.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the variance caused by process error, damage, shrinkage, or timing?
    • Does the variance exceed an approval threshold?
    • Is more investigation needed before approval?
  • Pain points:
    • Root causes are not always obvious.
    • The user may be balancing speed against control discipline.
    • Large variances can create pressure from multiple stakeholders.
  • Success outcome: Only justified variances move forward, preserving control and data accuracy.

12. Stock Adjustment

  • User role: Warehouse Manager
  • Goal: Correct recorded stock safely when reality does not match the system.
  • Steps:
    1. Open stock adjustment management.
    2. Identify the product and location.
    3. Enter increase or decrease quantity.
    4. Select the required reason code and add notes.
    5. Submit for approval if threshold rules require it.
    6. Confirm the adjustment is applied.
  • Decisions:
    • Is an adjustment truly needed or should the item be investigated first?
    • Which reason code best explains the change?
    • Does the value or quantity require independent approval?
  • Pain points:
    • Users may choose vague reason codes under time pressure.
    • Incorrect adjustments can worsen the data instead of fixing it.
    • Approval delays can block urgent corrections.
  • Success outcome: Stock is corrected with proper justification, traceability, and governance.

13. Inventory Write-Off

  • User role: Operations Director
  • Goal: Remove unsellable inventory in a controlled way with clear accountability.
  • Steps:
    1. Open pending write-off requests.
    2. Review the affected inventory, quantity, and supporting evidence.
    3. Check financial and operational implications.
    4. Approve or reject the write-off.
    5. Confirm finance acknowledgment if required.
    6. Complete write-off execution.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the inventory truly unsellable or should another disposition be used?
    • Is the evidence strong enough to support write-off?
    • Does finance need to review before final approval?
  • Pain points:
    • Write-offs can be sensitive and highly visible.
    • Weak documentation makes decisions harder.
    • Users may want better root-cause context before approval.
  • Success outcome: Unsellable stock is removed with defensible authorization and a full audit trail.

14. Quarantine and Hold Management

  • User role: Warehouse Manager
  • Goal: Prevent questionable or restricted stock from being used or sold until it is cleared.
  • Steps:
    1. Open quarantine and hold management.
    2. Locate the affected stock.
    3. Apply hold or quarantine status with a reason.
    4. Confirm the quantity is excluded from sellable stock.
    5. Monitor the hold until resolution.
    6. Release or disposition the stock when authorized.
  • Decisions:
    • Should the stock be quarantined, held temporarily, or written off?
    • How much quantity is affected?
    • Is the issue quality-related, regulatory, or operational?
  • Pain points:
    • Users need to move fast to avoid accidental sale or shipment.
    • Unclear ownership of follow-up can leave stock stuck in hold.
    • Long-running holds reduce usable inventory and frustrate teams.
  • Success outcome: Risky stock is contained quickly and kept out of normal operations until resolved.

15. Order Availability Confirmation

  • User role: Sales Representative
  • Goal: Determine whether the business can commit to a customer's requested order.
  • Steps:
    1. Open order availability confirmation.
    2. Review the requested products and quantities.
    3. Trigger an ATP check.
    4. Review line-by-line availability results.
    5. Consider location options or partial availability.
    6. Communicate the commitment position to the customer.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the order fully available, partially available, or unavailable?
    • Should the promise be made from one location or across the network?
    • Should the next step be reservation, split fulfillment, or backorder discussion?
  • Pain points:
    • Customer expectations are often immediate.
    • Users need clarity on what can actually be promised.
    • Network stock can complicate what seems like a simple answer.
  • Success outcome: The user gives a realistic and supportable commitment based on ATP, not guesswork.

16. Inventory Reservation

  • User role: Customer Service Representative
  • Goal: Reserve confirmed stock so it is protected for a specific customer order.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the confirmed order.
    2. Review availability and selected fulfillment location.
    3. Reserve the needed quantity.
    4. Confirm the reservation result.
    5. Release the order to warehouse fulfillment.
    6. Revisit the reservation later if the order changes.
  • Decisions:
    • Which location should fulfill the order?
    • Is there enough ATP for all lines?
    • Should a reservation be released if the customer changes or cancels the order?
  • Pain points:
    • Reservation mistakes can create downstream fulfillment issues.
    • Users need confidence that ATP is current at the moment of reservation.
    • Changing orders can require tedious reservation cleanup.
  • Success outcome: Stock is securely committed to the order and protected from double allocation.

17. Pick, Pack, and Ship

  • User role: Warehouse Picker / Packer
  • Goal: Fulfill the order accurately and get it shipped without causing stock errors.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the pick queue.
    2. Select the assigned order or task.
    3. Pick items from the indicated locations.
    4. Verify the picked products and quantities.
    5. Pack the shipment.
    6. Confirm shipment handoff and complete the task.
  • Decisions:
    • Does the shelf stock match what the task expects?
    • Is the picked quantity correct and complete?
    • If something is wrong, should the task be stopped and an exception raised?
  • Pain points:
    • Pick failures are disruptive and time-sensitive.
    • Staff need accurate location guidance to move fast.
    • Errors discovered late in packing waste effort and delay shipment.
  • Success outcome: The correct order is shipped accurately and inventory is deducted at the right moment.

18. Partial Fulfillment and Backorder Handling

  • User role: Customer Service Representative
  • Goal: Save as much of the order as possible when full quantity cannot be supplied immediately.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the affected order.
    2. Review available quantity versus ordered quantity.
    3. Discuss options with the customer.
    4. Record the customer's acceptance of a partial shipment if applicable.
    5. Confirm immediate fulfillment for available quantity.
    6. Create or monitor the backorder for the remainder.
  • Decisions:
    • Is partial shipment acceptable to the customer?
    • Should the remainder be backordered or canceled?
    • Is an expected future date credible enough to communicate?
  • Pain points:
    • Customer conversations can be sensitive and time-consuming.
    • Users may not always know when the remainder will be available.
    • Splitting an order adds coordination overhead.
  • Success outcome: The customer receives a clear, agreed plan and the available stock still moves forward.

19. Low-Stock Alert Review

  • User role: Purchasing Manager
  • Goal: Notice and prioritize stock risks early enough to prevent service problems.
  • Steps:
    1. Open low-stock alerts.
    2. Review active alerts by severity and product importance.
    3. Drill into the most urgent items.
    4. Check current stock, open supply, and network alternatives.
    5. Acknowledge each alert and assign next action.
    6. Monitor remaining unresolved alerts.
  • Decisions:
    • Which alert needs action first?
    • Should the answer be transfer, purchase, or watchful waiting?
    • Is the issue local or network-wide?
  • Pain points:
    • Too many alerts can create noise.
    • Users need enough context to act, not just know there is a problem.
    • Prioritization is harder when many SKUs are at risk simultaneously.
  • Success outcome: Critical alerts are acknowledged quickly and turned into concrete next actions.

20. Replenishment Planning

  • User role: Buyer
  • Goal: Convert stock signals into the right replenishment action at the right time.
  • Steps:
    1. Open replenishment planning.
    2. Review recommended reorder items.
    3. Check whether another location can cover the need first.
    4. Decide to create a requisition or take another action.
    5. Submit the requisition for approval.
    6. Follow it through to purchase order conversion.
  • Decisions:
    • Should the need be covered by transfer or purchase?
    • Is the recommended quantity appropriate?
    • Does the product remain eligible for reorder?
  • Pain points:
    • Users must balance urgency, cost, and available alternatives.
    • Data gaps in lead times or demand can reduce confidence.
    • Approval delay can keep urgent replenishment from moving fast enough.
  • Success outcome: A justified replenishment action is created and ready for procurement execution.

21. Inter-Location Transfer Request

  • User role: Regional / Store Manager
  • Goal: Solve a local shortage by using stock already available elsewhere in the network.
  • Steps:
    1. Open transfer request.
    2. Select destination location, source location, product, and quantity.
    3. Review source availability and transfer impact.
    4. Enter the business reason.
    5. Submit the request for approval.
    6. Track the request status.
  • Decisions:
    • Which source location can spare the stock?
    • Is transfer better than purchasing new stock?
    • Is the requested quantity appropriate and sustainable for the source?
  • Pain points:
    • Users may not always know the best source location.
    • Transfer urgency can conflict with approval latency.
    • Poor network visibility can lead to unnecessary transfers.
  • Success outcome: A well-justified transfer request is submitted to relieve the shortage with minimal network disruption.

22. Transfer Approval

  • User role: Operations Director
  • Goal: Approve only transfers that help the network without harming the source location.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the transfer approval queue.
    2. Review source and destination need.
    3. Check source stock after transfer.
    4. Decide to approve or reject.
    5. Record the decision.
    6. Notify locations through workflow status.
  • Decisions:
    • Will this transfer create a new risk at the source?
    • Is the shortage urgent enough to justify movement?
    • Should the request be approved as-is or rejected?
  • Pain points:
    • The approver must think network-wide, not locally.
    • Approval queues can become bottlenecks.
    • Incomplete justification makes confident decisions harder.
  • Success outcome: The best transfer requests move forward while risky ones are stopped before causing new problems.

23. Transfer Execution

  • User role: Warehouse Staff
  • Goal: Move stock from one location to another accurately and keep both locations' inventory correct.
  • Steps:
    1. Open approved transfer tasks.
    2. Pick the transfer quantity at the source.
    3. Verify and dispatch the stock.
    4. Send or hand off the stock for transport.
    5. Receive and verify it at the destination.
    6. Confirm completion of the transfer.
  • Decisions:
    • Does the picked quantity exactly match the transfer order?
    • Is any part of the stock damaged or mismatched during movement?
    • Can the destination accept the transfer as received?
  • Pain points:
    • Transfers have two operational handoffs, increasing failure risk.
    • In-transit gaps can create anxiety if status is unclear.
    • Errors at either end affect both source and destination records.
  • Success outcome: Stock leaves the source, arrives at the destination, and is fully traceable throughout the move.

24. Customer Return Authorization

  • User role: Customer Service Representative
  • Goal: Approve valid returns fairly while keeping control over what the warehouse should expect back.
  • Steps:
    1. Open return authorization.
    2. Find the original order.
    3. Select the item and quantity requested for return.
    4. Validate the reason and policy eligibility.
    5. Issue the return authorization.
    6. Share return instructions with the customer.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the return eligible under policy?
    • Is the requested quantity within allowed limits?
    • Should the authorization be issued or declined?
  • Pain points:
    • Users often need to balance customer satisfaction with policy compliance.
    • Missing order context slows the conversation.
    • Unclear reasons can make approval harder.
  • Success outcome: The customer gets a clear authorization path and the warehouse receives a controlled expectation of what will return.

25. Return Inspection and Disposition

  • User role: Receiving Clerk
  • Goal: Decide what to do with returned goods so good stock is recovered and bad stock is contained.
  • Steps:
    1. Open pending return receipts.
    2. Match the incoming return to its authorization.
    3. Verify quantity and product identity.
    4. Inspect physical condition.
    5. Choose disposition: restock, quarantine, or write-off.
    6. Confirm completion of the return process.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the return truly authorized?
    • Is the product resalable, damaged, or defective?
    • Should the stock go back into inventory, be held, or be removed?
  • Pain points:
    • Condition assessments can be subjective.
    • Returned goods may arrive incomplete or in poor condition.
    • Users need clarity on what qualifies for restock versus quarantine.
  • Success outcome: Returned goods are processed consistently and routed to the correct inventory state.

26. Reporting and Operational Review

  • User role: Operations Director
  • Goal: Understand operational performance and identify where intervention is needed.
  • Steps:
    1. Open reports and analytics.
    2. Choose the relevant report or dashboard.
    3. Filter by date, location, or category.
    4. Review trends, exceptions, and outliers.
    5. Drill into problem areas if needed.
    6. Export or share findings for follow-up action.
  • Decisions:
    • Which metric or report matters most right now?
    • Is this a one-off issue or a pattern?
    • Does the issue need operational action, policy change, or further investigation?
  • Pain points:
    • Large data sets can slow understanding if not well focused.
    • Users may struggle to connect metrics to actionable next steps.
    • Different stakeholders may need different levels of detail.
  • Success outcome: The user gains actionable insight and can direct operations based on evidence rather than instinct.

27. Inventory Valuation Reconciliation

  • User role: Finance Manager
  • Goal: Confirm that operational inventory records align with financial expectations for a period close.
  • Steps:
    1. Open valuation reconciliation.
    2. Select the relevant period.
    3. Review operational valuation and comparison figures.
    4. Investigate material variances.
    5. Document reconciliation notes.
    6. Finalize the period review.
  • Decisions:
    • Is the variance acceptable or material?
    • Does the issue stem from operations, timing, or finance treatment?
    • Can the period be closed with confidence?
  • Pain points:
    • Finance needs confidence in data produced by operational processes.
    • Large unexplained variances can create time pressure at period end.
    • Users may need to cross-check multiple underlying events.
  • Success outcome: Finance can complete reconciliation with a clear view of differences and documented closure confidence.

28. Promotional Stock Readiness

  • User role: Marketing Manager
  • Goal: Make sure enough inventory is secured before a campaign or launch commitment is made.
  • Steps:
    1. Open promotional readiness.
    2. Review campaign products and required quantities.
    3. Check ring-fenced stock, ATP, and inbound supply.
    4. Identify products at risk.
    5. Confirm readiness or escalate gaps.
    6. Communicate launch confidence to stakeholders.
  • Decisions:
    • Is current ring-fenced stock sufficient?
    • Can inbound supply close any shortfall in time?
    • Should the campaign proceed, be adjusted, or be escalated?
  • Pain points:
    • Promotional demand creates pressure on shared inventory.
    • Users need certainty before public commitments are made.
    • Gaps discovered late can disrupt campaigns and trust.
  • Success outcome: The campaign team has a credible readiness view and can commit with confidence.

29. Audit and Control Review

  • User role: Internal Auditor
  • Goal: Verify that inventory activity follows control rules and that the audit trail is complete.
  • Steps:
    1. Open the audit workspace.
    2. Define the audit scope.
    3. Review transactions, approvals, and control evidence.
    4. Sample high-risk records.
    5. Note findings, breaches, or clean results.
    6. Export evidence and complete the review.
  • Decisions:
    • Which locations, periods, or transaction types are highest risk?
    • Is a control failure isolated or systemic?
    • Does a finding require escalation or remediation tracking?
  • Pain points:
    • Audit users need complete, reliable history without ambiguity.
    • Missing approval evidence undermines trust quickly.
    • Investigations can be time-consuming when records are fragmented.
  • Success outcome: The auditor can confidently assess compliance and produce defensible findings.

30. User Account and Access Management

  • User role: System Administrator
  • Goal: Give each user the right access for their job while protecting control boundaries.
  • Steps:
    1. Open user account management.
    2. Search for an existing user or create a new one.
    3. Assign role and location scope.
    4. Review any access-control conflicts.
    5. Activate, suspend, or update the account as needed.
    6. Confirm effective permissions.
  • Decisions:
    • Does the user need a new account or an update to an existing one?
    • Which role best matches the user's responsibility?
    • Does the requested access create a segregation-of-duties issue?
  • Pain points:
    • Over-permissioning creates control risk.
    • Under-permissioning blocks operations and frustrates users.
    • Role complexity can make correct assignment difficult.
  • Success outcome: The user receives correct, scoped access that supports work without compromising governance.

Journey Design Notes

  • These journeys are intentionally written from the user's point of view rather than the system's.
  • The journeys can be used as input for task flows, wireframes, usability scenarios, and acceptance criteria.
  • Where multiple roles collaborate in one process, the journey is centered on the primary user who owns the outcome.

Inventory Management System User Flows

Purpose

This document defines user flows for each major feature of the Inventory Management System. The flows are screen-oriented and are intended to support UX design, wireframes, interaction design, and future usability validation.

Scope

The flows are based on the major features already identified across the BRD, use cases, screen inventory, navigation structure, and user journeys. Each flow includes:

  1. Starting screen
  2. User actions
  3. Navigation path
  4. Decision points
  5. Destination screen

Each flow is represented as a text-based diagram from the user's perspective.

1. Product Catalog Management

  • Starting screen: Home > Products > Product Catalog
  • User actions: Search product, create product, edit product, update status, save record
  • Navigation path: Product Catalog -> Product Detail / Create Product -> Save -> Product Detail
  • Decision points: New product or existing product? Duplicate detected? Active, inactive, or discontinued?
  • Destination screen: Product Detail
Product Catalog
  -> Search by SKU / name / category
  -> [Decision: Product exists?]
     -> No -> Create Product
           -> Enter product attributes
           -> [Decision: Duplicate detected?]
              -> Yes -> Review duplicate resolution
              -> No -> Save
           -> Product Detail
     -> Yes -> Product Detail
           -> Edit Product
           -> Update attributes / status
           -> Save
           -> Product Detail

  • Starting screen: Home > Products > Product Import
  • User actions: Download template, upload file, review validation, confirm import
  • Navigation path: Product Import -> Upload File -> Validation Results -> Import Completion
  • Decision points: File valid? Errors blocking import? Proceed with approved records only?
  • Destination screen: Import Completion
Product Import
  -> Upload File
  -> Validation Results
  -> [Decision: Validation passed?]
     -> No -> Correct file -> Re-upload
     -> Yes -> Confirm Import
           -> Import Completion

  • Decision points: New or existing location? Ready for activation? Opening balances complete?
  • Destination screen: Location Detail
Location Directory
  -> [Decision: Create new location?]
     -> Yes -> Create Location
           -> Enter location details
           -> Configure hierarchy
           -> Configure storage positions
           -> [Decision: Ready to activate?]
              -> No -> Save draft -> Location Detail
              -> Yes -> Activate Location
                     -> Location Detail
     -> No -> Location Detail
           -> Edit Hierarchy / Storage Positions / Status
           -> Save
           -> Location Detail

  -> Select approved transfer

  -> Pick and verify transfer stock
  -> Confirm dispatch
  -> Receipt Detail
  -> [Decision: Destination received full transfer?]
     -> No -> Investigate discrepancy
     -> Yes -> Confirm receipt
           -> Receipt Detail

33. Network Rebalancing Analysis

  • Starting screen: Home > Transfers > Network Rebalancing
  • User actions: Review imbalances, select recommendation, generate transfer request
  • Navigation path: Network Rebalancing -> Rebalancing Recommendation Detail -> Transfer Request
  • Decision points: Recommendation valid? Approve recommendation now?
  • Destination screen: Transfer Request Detail
Network Rebalancing
  -> Review imbalance dashboard
  -> Select recommendation
  -> Rebalancing Recommendation Detail
  -> [Decision: Approve recommendation?]
     -> No -> Return to dashboard
     -> Yes -> Generate transfer request
           -> Transfer Request Detail

34. Return Authorization Management

  • Starting screen: Home > Returns > Return Authorizations
  • User actions: Search order, validate return, issue authorization
  • Navigation path: Return Authorizations -> Return Authorization Detail -> Issue authorization
  • Decision points: Return eligible? Quantity allowed? Approve return?
  • Destination screen: Return Authorization Detail
Return Authorizations
  -> Search original order
  -> Return Authorization Detail
  -> Select items and quantity
  -> Validate return reason / policy
  -> [Decision: Eligible return?]
     -> No -> Decline request
     -> Yes -> Issue authorization
           -> Return Authorization Detail

35. Return Inspection and Disposition

  • Starting screen: Home > Returns > Return Inspection & Disposition
  • User actions: Receive return, inspect item, select disposition
  • Navigation path: Return Inspection & Disposition -> Return Receipt Detail -> Inspection Detail -> Disposition Detail
  • Decision points: Authorized return? Resalable, quarantine, or write-off?
  • Destination screen: Disposition Detail
Return Inspection & Disposition
  -> Select pending return
  -> Return Receipt Detail
  -> Verify received quantity
  -> Inspection Detail
  -> Assess condition
  -> [Decision: Disposition?]
     -> Restock -> Confirm restock
     -> Quarantine -> Quarantine & Holds
     -> Write-off -> Write-Off Authorization Detail
  -> Disposition Detail

36. Operational Reports and Analytics

  • Starting screen: Home > Reports & Analytics > Operational Reports
  • User actions: Select report, filter results, drill down, export
  • Navigation path: Operational Reports -> Report View -> Detail / Export
  • Decision points: Which report? Need drill-down? Export needed?
  • Destination screen: Report View
Operational Reports
  -> Select report type
  -> Report View
  -> Apply filters
  -> Review results
  -> [Decision: Need drill-down?]
     -> Yes -> Detail View
     -> No -> Continue
  -> [Decision: Export report?]
     -> Yes -> Export
     -> No -> Report View

37. Executive KPI Dashboard

  • Starting screen: Home > Executive KPI Dashboard

  • Navigation path: Executive KPI Dashboard -> KPI Detail -> Supporting report
  • Decision points: KPI on target? Drill into underperformance?
  • Destination screen: KPI Detail or supporting analytics view
Executive KPI Dashboard
  -> Select reporting period
  -> Review KPIs and trends
  -> [Decision: KPI underperforming?]
     -> No -> Continue review
     -> Yes -> KPI Detail
           -> Open supporting report / analysis

38. Inventory Valuation Reconciliation

  • Starting screen: Home > Reports & Analytics > Valuation Reconciliation
  • User actions: Select period, compare values, document notes, finalize
  • Navigation path: Valuation Reconciliation -> Reconciliation Detail -> Finalize
  • Decision points: Variance acceptable? Need deeper investigation?
  • Destination screen: Reconciliation Detail
Valuation Reconciliation
  -> Select period
  -> Reconciliation Detail
  -> Compare operational vs finance view
  -> [Decision: Variance within tolerance?]
     -> Yes -> Finalize reconciliation
     -> No -> Investigate underlying drivers
           -> Document notes
           -> Finalize or escalate

39. Promotional Stock Readiness

  • Starting screen: Home > Reports & Analytics > Promotional Readiness
  • User actions: Open campaign, review readiness, confirm or escalate
  • Navigation path: Promotional Readiness -> Campaign Detail -> Confirm readiness / Escalate
  • Decision points: Stock sufficient? Inbound closes gap? Ready to confirm?
  • Destination screen: Campaign Detail
Promotional Readiness
  -> Select campaign
  -> Campaign Detail
  -> Review allocated / ring-fenced / inbound supply
  -> [Decision: Campaign stock ready?]
     -> No -> Escalate gap / update plan
     -> Yes -> Confirm readiness
           -> Campaign Detail

40. Audit Workspace

  • Starting screen: Home > Governance & Audit > Audit Workspace
  • User actions: Define scope, review records, document findings, export evidence
  • Navigation path: Audit Workspace -> Audit Review Detail -> Export
  • Decision points: Control issue found? Sample more records? Export evidence?
  • Destination screen: Audit Review Detail
Audit Workspace
  -> Define scope
  -> Audit Review Detail
  -> Review transactions / approvals / controls
  -> [Decision: Finding identified?]
     -> No -> Continue sampling / close review
     -> Yes -> Document finding
  -> [Decision: Export evidence?]
     -> Yes -> Export package
     -> No -> Audit Review Detail

41. Audit Trail Query

  • Starting screen: Home > Governance & Audit > Audit Trail Query
  • User actions: Enter search criteria, review log entries, inspect record details, export
  • Navigation path: Audit Trail Query -> Audit Record Detail -> Export
  • Decision points: Results found? Need before/after detail? Export required?
  • Destination screen: Audit Record Detail
Audit Trail Query
  -> Enter search criteria
  -> Review results
  -> [Decision: Matching records found?]
     -> No -> Refine search
     -> Yes -> Audit Record Detail
           -> Review before / after state
           -> [Decision: Export results?]
              -> Yes -> Export
              -> No -> Audit Record Detail

42. User Account Management

  • Starting screen: Home > Administration > User Accounts
  • User actions: Create user, edit user, assign role, suspend or deactivate account
  • Navigation path: User Accounts -> User Account Detail -> Save / Suspend / Deactivate
  • Decision points: New or existing user? Change role? Suspend or deactivate?
  • Destination screen: User Account Detail
User Accounts
  -> Search user
  -> [Decision: Existing user?]
     -> No -> Create User
           -> Enter profile and scope
           -> Save
           -> User Account Detail
     -> Yes -> User Account Detail
           -> Edit user / assign role / change scope
           -> [Decision: Suspend or deactivate?]
              -> Suspend -> Confirm -> User Account Detail
              -> Deactivate -> Confirm -> User Account Detail
              -> Neither -> Save changes -> User Account Detail

43. Roles and Access Control

  • Starting screen: Home > Administration > Roles & Access Control
  • User actions: Open role, review permissions, update scope rules, save
  • Navigation path: Roles & Access Control -> Role Permission Detail -> Save
  • Decision points: Permission conflict? Location scope valid? SoD breach?
  • Destination screen: Role Permission Detail
Roles & Access Control
  -> Select role
  -> Role Permission Detail
  -> Review permissions and location scope
  -> [Decision: SoD conflict detected?]
     -> Yes -> Revise permissions / scope
     -> No -> Save
           -> Role Permission Detail

Notes

  • These flows focus on major features rather than every minor interaction.
  • Flows are aligned to previously defined screens and navigation structure.
  • The diagrams can be used directly as the basis for task flows, page transitions, and low-fidelity UX design.

Inventory Management System Low-Fidelity Wireframe Specifications

Purpose

This document defines low-fidelity wireframe specifications for every identified Inventory Management System screen. The specifications are text-based and describe structural content only. They do not define visual styling, spacing, branding, or high-fidelity interaction behavior.

Structure Standard

Each screen specification includes:

  1. Header
  2. Navigation
  3. Main content
  4. Forms
  5. Tables
  6. Action buttons
  7. Footer (if applicable)

Shared Layout Assumptions

  • The application uses a persistent top header.
  • Main navigation is available globally.
  • Secondary navigation appears at module level when applicable.
  • Breadcrumbs appear below the header on all non-home screens.
  • Most operational screens use a list-detail or dashboard-workbench structure.
  • Footer is optional and used mainly for system metadata, help links, and record timestamps.

Notes

  • These specifications are intentionally structural and low-fidelity.
  • They should be used to create wireframes, not as final UI designs.
  • Screen-level interaction states such as empty, loading, error, and success states should be added during detailed wireframe and prototype work.

Inventory Management System Form Specifications and Validation

Purpose

This document defines the UX form specification for every major form in the Inventory Management System. It aligns user-facing validation, inline behavior, success behavior, and error behavior with the approved API validation and error specifications in:

  • SRS/API_Design/Request-DTO-Validation-Spec.md
  • SRS/API_Design/Error-Response-Specification.md

Scope Notes

  • This document focuses on application forms, not read-only dashboards or query-only screens with no editable input.
  • Where multiple screens use the same underlying form pattern, a single shared form specification is used.
  • Validation messages are written for users but remain aligned to backend rules such as VAL_*, BIZ_*, CONF_*, and supporting VR-xxx / BR-xxx rules.
  • Input types are expressed in UX terms such as text field, dropdown, date picker, numeric field, file upload, and checkbox.

Shared Validation Behavior

These rules apply to all forms unless a form-specific rule overrides them.

Inline Validation Behavior

  • Validate required fields on blur and on submit.
  • Validate format-sensitive fields on blur once the user leaves the field.
  • Validate cross-field rules when any dependent field changes.
  • Do not show an error before the user has interacted with a field, except after submit.
  • Replace blocking field errors with success/neutral state immediately when corrected.
  • For numeric quantity and amount fields, enforce allowed precision in the input where practical and confirm again on blur.
  • For code fields such as SKU, Location Code, Supplier Code, and Reason Code, preserve uppercase formatting where the API expects uppercase patterns.

Success Behavior

  • After successful submit, show a visible success banner with a concise outcome statement.
  • Keep the user on the record detail screen for create/update forms unless the workflow naturally returns to a queue.
  • Refresh related summary panels, tables, and status badges immediately after success.
  • For multi-step or queued work, mark the completed item as processed and move the user to the next logical task.

Error Behavior

  • For 400 VAL_* errors, map field-level errors inline and show a form-level summary banner.
  • For 409 CONF_* errors, keep user-entered values intact and explain the conflicting record or state.
  • For 422 BIZ_* errors, show a form-level business-rule message and highlight any affected fields or sections.
  • For 401 AUTH_* errors, redirect to re-authentication or session recovery flow.
  • For 403 AUTHZ_* errors, disable retry-only behavior and explain that the user lacks access.
  • For 500/503 SYS_* errors, preserve draft state when possible and offer retry behavior.

Standard Form-Level Error Summary Pattern

  • Title: There is a problem with this form.
  • Body: Review the highlighted fields and try again.
  • If the API returns traceId, show it in support-facing error details but not as primary user content.

Shared Field Patterns

Shared Pattern A: Product SKU

  • Input type: Single-line text field
  • Required fields: Required when the form creates, updates, or references a specific product
  • Validation messages:
    • SKU is required.
    • SKU must use uppercase letters, numbers, hyphens, or underscores only.
    • SKU cannot be longer than 50 characters.
    • This product could not be found. (NF_PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND)
  • Inline validation behavior: Convert to uppercase on blur where appropriate; validate pattern ^[A-Z0-9][A-Z0-9_-]*$.

Shared Pattern B: Location Code

  • Input type: Searchable dropdown or code text field depending on context
  • Required fields: Required when location-scoped activity occurs
  • Validation messages:
    • Location is required.
    • Select a valid location.
    • You are not authorized for this location. (AUTHZ_LOCATION_SCOPE_DENIED)
  • Inline validation behavior: Validate existence and scope after selection when API lookup is available.

Shared Pattern C: Quantity

  • Input type: Numeric decimal field with unit label
  • Required fields: Required when stock, order, receipt, or transfer quantity is submitted
  • Validation messages:
    • Quantity is required.
    • Quantity must be greater than 0. for positive quantity contexts
    • Quantity cannot be negative.
    • Quantity has too many decimal places.
    • Quantity exceeds the allowed available amount. (BIZ_INSUFFICIENT_ATP, BIZ_SOURCE_MINIMUM_PROTECTED, or context equivalent)
  • Inline validation behavior: Validate numeric format immediately; validate business ceilings after related context fields are complete.

Shared Pattern D: Reason Code

  • Input type: Dropdown
  • Required fields: Required for adjustments, write-offs, discrepancies, holds, and many exception flows
  • Validation messages:
    • Reason code is required.
    • Select a valid active reason code.
    • This reason code cannot be used for this transaction type.
  • Inline validation behavior: Filter reason-code options by transaction type where possible.

Shared Pattern E: Date Range

  • Input type: Start date + end date date pickers
  • Required fields: Required for reporting and audit forms where specified
  • Validation messages:
    • Start date is required.
    • End date is required.
    • Start date must be on or before end date. (VAL_INVALID_DATE_RANGE)
    • The selected date range is too large for this request.
  • Inline validation behavior: Revalidate both fields whenever either date changes.

Form Specifications

F-001 Sign In Form

  • Related screens: UI-001
  • Aligned APIs: Session/auth integration, API-173, API-174

Fields

Field Input type Required
Username / Email Text field Yes
Password Password field Yes
Remember Session Checkbox No

Validation messages

  • Username or email is required.
  • Password is required.
  • Your session could not be started. Check your credentials and try again. (AUTH_INVALID_TOKEN equivalent UX messaging)
  • Your account is suspended. (AUTH_ACCOUNT_SUSPENDED)
  • Your account is deactivated. (AUTH_ACCOUNT_DEACTIVATED)

Inline validation behavior

  • Required validation on blur and submit.
  • Password field does not show content-specific validation, only presence.

Success behavior

  • Redirect to Operational Home Dashboard or role-specific landing page.

Error behavior

  • Authentication failures show a form-level error banner.
  • Preserve entered username/email after failure; clear password field.

F-002 Product Form

  • Related screens: UI-005
  • Aligned APIs: API-001, API-004, API-005

Fields

Field Input type Required
SKU Text field Yes on create
Name Text field Yes
Description Text area No
Unit of Measure Dropdown Yes
Category Code Searchable dropdown No
Barcode Text field No
Is Traceable Toggle No
Rotation Policy Dropdown Conditional
Shelf Life Managed Toggle No
MRSL Threshold Days Numeric field Conditional
Lifecycle Status Dropdown Yes on edit/status action
Status Change Reason Text area No
Effective Date Date picker No

Validation messages

  • SKU is required.
  • SKU must use uppercase letters, numbers, hyphens, or underscores only.
  • SKU cannot be longer than 50 characters.
  • A product with this SKU already exists. (CONF_DUPLICATE_SKU)
  • Name is required.
  • Name cannot be longer than 200 characters.
  • Unit of measure is required.
  • Barcode cannot be longer than 50 characters.
  • A product with this barcode already exists. (CONF_DUPLICATE_BARCODE)
  • Rotation policy is required when the product is traceable.
  • MRSL threshold days is required when shelf life management is enabled.
  • MRSL threshold days must be at least 1.
  • Select a valid lifecycle status.
  • This lifecycle change is not allowed for the current product state.

Inline validation behavior

  • SKU: uppercase normalization, pattern validation on blur.
  • Conditional fields appear and become required immediately when toggles are enabled.
  • Duplicate SKU/barcode checks can run after blur if asynchronous validation is available.

Success behavior

  • Show success banner: Product saved successfully.
  • Remain on Product Detail.

Error behavior

  • 400 field errors map inline.
  • 409 duplicate conflicts show inline on SKU or barcode and in banner.
  • 422 lifecycle/business-rule failures show form-level message and keep values intact.

Inline validation behavior

Error behavior

  • Entire-request validation issues show form-level error.
  • Per-row errors stay in the results grid with row-level messages.

  • Select at least one permission for this role.
  • Approver cannot be the same as the initiator. (BIZ_SEGREGATION_OF_DUTIES)
  • Select a valid transaction type for segregation-of-duties evaluation.
  • You are not authorized to assign this role. (AUTHZ_ROLE_ASSIGNMENT_DENIED)

Inline validation behavior

  • SoD evaluation can run when both users and transaction type are present.
  • Permission matrix should show conflict/warning state before save where possible.

Success behavior

  • Permission matrix saves and confirmation banner appears.

Error behavior

  • Keep all edited permission changes in memory until user chooses to discard or retry.

F-049 Session / Logout Form

  • Related screens: Global user menu
  • Aligned APIs: API-174

Fields

Field Input type Required
Logout All Sessions Checkbox No

Validation messages

  • None beyond system-level failure messaging

Inline validation behavior

  • No inline validation required

Success behavior

  • End session and redirect to sign-in screen

Error behavior

  • If logout fails, show lightweight banner and allow retry

Traceability Summary

  • Product, catalog, and lifecycle forms align primarily to VR-001 to VR-010.
  • Location and storage forms align primarily to VR-011 to VR-017.
  • Stock policy, governance, and threshold forms align primarily to VR-018 to VR-028.
  • Procurement and supplier forms align primarily to VR-030 to VR-051.
  • Receiving and discrepancy forms align primarily to VR-035 to VR-048.
  • Fulfillment forms align primarily to VR-090 to VR-111.
  • Replenishment and transfer forms align primarily to VR-117 to VR-141.
  • Returns forms align primarily to VR-142 to VR-149.
  • Reporting and audit date-range forms align primarily to VR-062, VR-153, and related intelligence query rules.
  • User and access forms align primarily to VR-083 and location-scope validations such as VR-008 and VR-053.

Notes

  • This specification is written for UX and frontend implementation and should be read together with the backend validation and error contracts.
  • Final field-level implementation should preserve API naming, value constraints, and business-rule enforcement even if labels are simplified for users.
  • Empty, loading, disabled, and async-check states should be specified in the next UI interaction-state pass.

Inventory Management System Screen State Specifications

Purpose

This document defines the expected user experience for key screen states across every Inventory Management System screen. It covers:

  1. Loading state
  2. Empty state
  3. Error state
  4. Success state
  5. No-permission state

The goal is to ensure every screen behaves consistently and gives users clear guidance when data is loading, absent, successful, blocked, or unavailable.

Shared UX Principles

  • Loading: Preserve page structure with skeletons or placeholders so users understand what is coming.
  • Empty: Explain why nothing is shown and what the user can do next.
  • Error: State what went wrong in user language, preserve work where possible, and offer recovery.
  • Success: Confirm completion clearly and update the affected data or workflow immediately.
  • No-permission: Explain access limits without exposing sensitive detail and point users to the right next action.

UI-001 Sign In / Session Entry

Loading state

  • Show a disabled sign-in button with inline spinner after submit.
  • Keep username visible and mask password.
  • Message: Signing you in...

Empty state

  • Not applicable as a data state.
  • Default first-load experience acts as the neutral state.

Error state

  • Show a form-level error for invalid credentials or session problems.
  • Preserve username/email; clear password.
  • Offer retry and help link.

Success state

  • Show brief transition feedback such as Sign-in successful.
  • Redirect immediately to the correct landing screen.

No-permission state

  • If authentication succeeds but the account has no usable access, show:
    • Your account is active, but no application access has been assigned.
    • Action: Contact Administrator

UI-002 Operational Home Dashboard

Loading state

  • Show skeleton KPI cards, placeholder alert rows, and shortcut tile skeletons.
  • Keep page header and navigation visible.

Empty state

  • If there are no alerts or tasks, show:
    • You are up to date.
    • Explain that no urgent items or pending tasks exist.

Error state

  • Show banner: We could not load the dashboard right now.
  • Keep navigation available.
  • Offer Retry.

Success state

  • After refresh or task completion, show a non-blocking success banner:
    • Dashboard updated successfully.

No-permission state

  • If user can access home but not some widgets, show available widgets and replace restricted ones with:
    • You do not have access to this data.

UI-003 Executive KPI Dashboard

Loading state

  • Show KPI card skeletons and trend placeholders.
  • Preserve selected period if already chosen.

Empty state

  • Show:
    • No KPI data is available for the selected period.
    • Suggest changing period or scope.

Error state

  • Show banner: KPI data could not be loaded.
  • Keep filters intact.
  • Offer Retry.

Success state

  • After filters change, update KPI cards and show subtle confirmation:
    • Dashboard updated.

No-permission state

  • Show:
    • You do not have permission to view executive KPI data.
    • Offer return to Home.

UI-004 Notification Center

Loading state

  • Show placeholder notification rows and a blank detail pane with shimmer state.

Empty state

  • Show:
    • No notifications to review.
    • Explain that alerts, approvals, and operational notices will appear here.

Error state

  • Show:
    • Notifications could not be loaded.
    • Preserve current filters if any.

Success state

  • After acknowledge/handle:
    • Remove or update the item in place.
    • Show Notification updated.

No-permission state

  • Show:
    • You do not have permission to view this notification set.
    • If partial access exists, show only allowed items.

UI-005 Product Catalog Management

Loading state

  • Show product table skeleton and product detail placeholder.
  • Keep search/filter bar visible.

Empty state

  • If catalog is empty:
    • No products have been created yet.
    • Primary action: Create Product
  • If search returns no matches:
    • No products match these filters.

Error state

  • For catalog load failure:
    • Products could not be loaded.
  • For save failure:
    • Preserve form values and show inline plus banner errors.

Success state

  • After create/update:
    • Show Product saved successfully.
    • Refresh detail and table row.

No-permission state

  • Read-only users see product data without edit actions.
  • Fully blocked users see:
    • You do not have permission to manage products.

UI-006 Product Import Workspace

Loading state

Empty state

  • Show:
    • No import file uploaded yet.

Error state

  • If file-level failure:
    • The import could not be processed.
  • If validation fails:
    • Keep file summary and display row-level issues clearly.

Success state

  • Show created/updated counts and any non-blocking warnings.
  • Message: Import completed successfully.

No-permission state

  • Show:
    • You do not have permission to import product data.
    • Hide upload control.

Success state

  • Location activated successfully. or equivalent action-specific feedback.

No-permission state

  • Show read-only location directory if view-only access exists.
  • Otherwise show blocked-state message with return navigation.

Inventory Management System UI Guidelines

Purpose

This document defines UI guidelines for the Inventory Management System covering responsiveness, accessibility, keyboard interaction, and mobile behavior. The recommendations are aligned to WCAG principles of being:

  • Perceivable
  • Operable
  • Understandable
  • Robust

The guidance is intended for UX, UI, frontend engineering, QA, and accessibility review.

Accessibility Target

The recommended baseline target for the IMS is:

  • WCAG 2.2 AA for all core user journeys

This is especially important because the system is used for:

  • Time-sensitive warehouse operations
  • Data-entry-heavy workflows
  • Multi-role enterprise access
  • Reporting and audit use cases

1. Responsive Breakpoints

Design Intent

The IMS is primarily a business web application used on desktop and laptop devices, but it should remain usable on tablets and selectively on mobile for read-heavy and lightweight task flows. Complex data-entry and table-heavy workflows should remain optimized for larger screens.

Recommended Breakpoints

Breakpoint Width Primary Usage
xs 0-479px Small mobile phones
sm 480-767px Large phones / small mobile landscape
md 768-1023px Tablets / small laptops
lg 1024-1439px Standard laptops / desktop
xl 1440px+ Large desktop / wide operational monitors

Layout Guidance by Breakpoint

xs and sm

  • Use a single-column layout.
  • Collapse secondary navigation into drawers, accordions, or segmented tabs.
  • Move filter bars into expandable panels.
  • Stack form fields vertically.
  • Replace dense multi-column tables with card-list or priority-column responsive tables.
  • Limit simultaneous pane layouts; avoid side-by-side master-detail patterns unless converted to drill-in navigation.

md

  • Allow two-panel layouts selectively.
  • Keep primary navigation collapsible.
  • Use horizontally scrollable tables only when card conversion would lose too much structure.
  • Preserve important workbench workflows where possible, but simplify dense controls.

lg and xl

  • Use full enterprise layout with:
    • persistent global header
    • primary navigation
    • secondary navigation
    • list-detail and workbench layouts
  • Allow wider tables, multi-column forms, and parallel information panels.

Responsive Rules

  • Never rely on hover-only interaction at any breakpoint.
  • Do not hide critical actions inside unstable overflow patterns without a clear alternative.
  • Avoid fixed-height panels that trap content at smaller sizes.
  • Preserve task order when stacking columns vertically.
  • Ensure zoom to 200% does not break essential workflows.

WCAG Alignment

  • Supports Perceivable and Operable principles by maintaining content access across viewport sizes and zoom states.

2. Keyboard Navigation

Design Intent

All essential tasks must be operable using a keyboard alone, especially because IMS users may:

  • perform repetitive data entry
  • use barcode/scanner-assisted input
  • work quickly in operational contexts
  • need non-pointer accessibility support

Core Requirements

  • All interactive controls must be reachable with Tab.
  • Use Shift + Tab for backward movement in a predictable order.
  • Ensure visible focus on every interactive element.
  • All actions available by mouse must also be available by keyboard.
  • Avoid keyboard traps.

Expected Keyboard Behavior

Global

  • Tab moves through interactive elements in reading/task order.
  • Enter activates primary buttons and selected menu items.
  • Space toggles checkboxes, switches, and some buttons where appropriate.
  • Esc closes dialogs, menus, drawers, and temporary overlays.

Navigation

  • Menus, tabs, accordions, and dropdowns must support arrow-key navigation where standard patterns apply.
  • Breadcrumb links must be keyboard reachable.
  • Skip link should be available to jump to main content.

Forms

  • Entering data should not unexpectedly submit multi-field forms.
  • Inline validation must not steal keyboard focus unless the user submits and an error summary intentionally redirects focus.

Tables and Grids

  • Row actions must be reachable via keyboard.
  • Sortable headers must be operable by keyboard.
  • Expandable rows must support Enter or Space.
  • If grid-like interactions are used, arrow-key behavior must be consistent and documented.

Keyboard Priority Areas in IMS

Special attention is required for:

  • Goods Receipt Workbench
  • Put-Away Workbench
  • Cycle Count Workbench
  • Pick, Pack, and Ship Workbench
  • Stock Adjustment Management
  • User Account Management

WCAG Alignment

  • Supports Operable principle, especially keyboard accessibility and predictable interaction.

3. Focus Management

Design Intent

Focus must move intentionally so users always know where they are, what changed, and what to do next.

Global Focus Rules

  • On page load, focus should move to the page heading or main content container, not remain ambiguously in the browser chrome.
  • Do not move focus unexpectedly during normal typing or filtering.
  • When opening a modal, drawer, or popup, move focus into it.
  • When closing a modal, return focus to the triggering control.
  • When a page update occurs after a submit, direct focus to the most relevant next element:
    • success banner
    • first validation error
    • updated record heading

Error Focus Rules

  • On failed submit, move focus to the error summary if present.
  • The error summary should include links or relationships to invalid fields.
  • Focus should then allow the user to move naturally into each field error.

Success Focus Rules

  • For save/update actions that remain on the same page, focus should move to:

    • success banner, then
    • updated record title or first relevant next action

  • For create flows that navigate to a detail page, focus should land on the new page heading.

Dynamic Content Rules

  • When filters refresh results asynchronously, do not steal focus from the current control unless the user explicitly triggers navigation into results.
  • If an item disappears from a queue after success, move focus to:
    • the next logical row, or
    • the list heading if the queue becomes empty

Dialog and Overlay Rules

  • Focus must be trapped within active modals.
  • Background content must not be keyboard reachable while modal is open.
  • Closing the overlay restores prior focus context.

WCAG Alignment

  • Supports Operable and Understandable principles through predictable navigation and state transitions.

4. Color Contrast

Design Intent

Color must support meaning, not carry meaning alone. IMS screens use many statuses, alerts, thresholds, and workflow states, so contrast and redundant cues are critical.

Minimum Contrast Recommendations

  • Normal text: 4.5:1 minimum
  • Large text: 3:1 minimum
  • Essential UI components and icons: 3:1 minimum against adjacent colors
  • Focus indicators: clearly visible with 3:1 minimum contrast against surrounding colors

Status and Semantic Guidance

Status indicators such as:

  • low stock
  • out of stock
  • quarantined
  • approved
  • rejected
  • delayed
  • at risk

must not rely on color alone.

Use at least one of:

  • text labels
  • icons
  • patterns
  • badges
  • helper text

Example:

  • Not just red dot
  • Use: Out of Stock badge with icon and accessible text

Background and Surface Guidance

  • Avoid placing light text on low-contrast tinted cards.
  • Avoid thin gray text in metadata areas if it drops below accessibility thresholds.
  • Ensure disabled state still remains readable enough to understand context, while clearly differentiated from enabled state.

Charts and Data Visualization

  • Use more than color to distinguish series:
    • labels
    • patterns
    • markers
    • direct annotations
  • Ensure chart legends are keyboard and screen-reader understandable where interactive.

WCAG Alignment

  • Supports Perceivable principle through sufficient visual contrast and non-color-dependent communication.

5. Form Accessibility

Design Intent

Forms are central to the IMS, especially for inventory transactions, approvals, receiving, fulfillment, and administration. They must be accessible, efficient, and forgiving.

Labeling Rules

  • Every input must have a persistent visible label.
  • Placeholder text must not replace labels.
  • Required fields must be clearly identified visually and programmatically.
  • Optional fields may be marked explicitly if that reduces ambiguity.

Instruction and Help Rules

  • Put concise helper text near the field when needed.
  • Use examples only if they clarify format.
  • Keep field guidance short and specific.

Validation Rules

  • Field errors must be programmatically associated with the field.
  • Error text must explain:
    • what is wrong
    • how to fix it
  • Validation must not depend only on color.
  • Use clear language like:
    • Quantity must be greater than 0
    • not: Invalid value

Grouping Rules

  • Related controls should be grouped with clear section headings.
  • Radio groups and checkbox groups should be wrapped in accessible group semantics.
  • Repeating line-item forms must expose row and field context clearly.

Input Behavior Rules

  • Use appropriate input types:
    • email for email
    • numeric fields for quantities
    • date pickers for dates
  • Support manual entry in addition to picker-only interactions where practical.
  • Avoid requiring drag-only or pointer-only actions.

Required Accessibility Features

  • Labels linked to controls
  • Error text linked to controls
  • Required state announced to assistive technology
  • Disabled/read-only states distinguishable programmatically
  • Autosave or draft patterns must not interrupt screen reader flow unexpectedly

Form-Specific IMS Priorities

Special care is needed for:

  • line-item editors
  • barcode/scanner-assisted fields
  • conditional fields
  • approval decision sections
  • multi-step receiving and return workflows

WCAG Alignment

  • Supports Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust principles.

6. Table Accessibility

Design Intent

Tables are one of the most heavily used patterns in the IMS. They must support scanning, sorting, selection, and row actions without becoming inaccessible.

Structural Rules

  • Use true table semantics for tabular data.
  • Header cells must be properly associated with their columns.
  • Complex tables with grouped headers should preserve readable relationships.

Interaction Rules

  • Sortable columns must indicate current sort state.
  • Row selection checkboxes must have clear labels.
  • Row action menus must be keyboard and screen-reader accessible.
  • Expandable rows must announce expanded/collapsed state.

Content Rules

  • Keep column names concise and descriptive.
  • Do not truncate essential meaning without a way to access full content.
  • Numeric values should be aligned consistently for readability, but semantic structure must remain intact.

Responsive Table Rules

On smaller screens:

  • prioritize critical columns
  • allow horizontal scrolling only when necessary
  • consider card transformation for highly dense operational lists
  • preserve access to row actions and identifiers

Empty and Error Rules

  • Empty tables should clearly explain that there are no records, not simply show blank space.
  • Loading tables should use skeleton rows.
  • Error states should appear above the table and allow retry.

High-Priority IMS Table Types

Special care is needed for:

  • inventory status tables
  • purchase order line tables
  • receipt line tables
  • order line status tables
  • transfer and approval queues
  • audit logs
  • permission matrices

WCAG Alignment

  • Supports Perceivable, Operable, and Understandable principles for structured data access.

7. Mobile Considerations

Design Intent

The IMS should support mobile selectively. Not every desktop workflow should be forced into a full mobile experience. The mobile strategy should prioritize:

  • lookup tasks
  • lightweight approvals
  • notifications
  • simple updates
  • selected warehouse actions where practical

Suitable Mobile-First or Mobile-Friendly Tasks

  • notifications
  • approvals
  • stock lookup
  • order status inquiry
  • low-stock alert review
  • basic return receipt steps
  • simple transfer confirmation

Desktop-Preferred Tasks

These should remain optimized for tablet/desktop due to complexity:

  • purchase order editing with many lines
  • large discrepancy resolution
  • detailed physical counts
  • complex inventory adjustment cases
  • valuation reconciliation
  • permission matrix editing
  • audit review with large datasets

Mobile Interaction Rules

  • Use larger tap targets.
  • Avoid hover-only actions.
  • Keep one primary action visible at a time.
  • Use sticky bottom action areas sparingly and only when they do not cover content.
  • Favor drill-down flows over multi-pane layouts.
  • Use clear back navigation and preserve entered data when moving between screens.

Mobile Form Rules

  • Keep forms short and segmented.
  • Reduce side-by-side fields.
  • Use mobile-friendly input controls where appropriate.
  • Ensure scanners or hardware keyboards do not break focus order.

Mobile Table Rules

  • Convert dense tables into stacked cards where needed.
  • Keep record ID, status, and primary action visible.
  • Hide secondary metadata behind expand/collapse patterns if necessary.

Orientation and Zoom

  • Support portrait-first for phones.
  • Avoid requiring landscape for essential tasks unless the task is explicitly desktop/tablet-only.
  • Ensure users can zoom without clipping essential controls.

WCAG Alignment

  • Supports Operable and Perceivable principles by preserving access under touch, zoom, and small-screen constraints.

8. Additional WCAG-Aligned Recommendations

Language and Clarity

  • Use plain, task-oriented labels.
  • Keep system messages specific and actionable.
  • Avoid unexplained abbreviations unless they are common in the user domain and defined consistently.

Time and Session

  • Warn users before session timeout where data entry may be lost.
  • Provide recovery options for long-running forms.
